title: Bending Light: Reflection & Refraction
summary: Bend mirrors and lenses by hand to discover how reflection, refraction, and total internal reflection actually work.
theory: Light travels in straight lines until it meets a new surface, where it obeys one of two rules. **Reflection**: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; curving the mirror (concave) gathers parallel rays to a single **principal focus (F)**, related to the radius of curvature by f = R/2. **Refraction**: light changes speed crossing between media, bending its path according to Snell's Law, n = sin i / sin r. A convex lens uses this to focus light to a point whose position depends on the object distance u relative to f (1/v − 1/u = 1/f). When light inside a denser medium hits a boundary steeper than the **critical angle** (sin θc = 1/n), it undergoes **total internal reflection** and cannot escape at all — the principle behind optical fibres.

procedure.title: Bend the concave mirror
procedure.description: Drag the glowing ring on the mirror's rim to change its curvature and watch the focal point F move.

procedure.title: Find the burning point
procedure.description: Slide the paper screen until it sits exactly at F and observe what happens; then switch to bulb mode and place the bulb at F to produce a parallel beam.

procedure.title: Squash the convex lens
procedure.description: Drag the candle and the lens, and use the bulge handle to change the lens's focal length. Note how the image changes from real & inverted to virtual & magnified as the candle crosses F.

procedure.title: Find the critical angle
procedure.description: Drag the torch inside the glass/water/diamond block and sweep the angle until the beam suddenly stops escaping — that is the critical angle, and beyond it you get total internal reflection.

procedure.title: Build an instrument
procedure.description: On the optician's bench, arrange the two lenses and the object to complete each mission: a telescope, a microscope, and a projector.

observation: The mirror's focal length shortens as its curvature deepens, matching f = R/2. The lens image flips from real/inverted to virtual/magnified exactly when the object crosses the focal point. Total internal reflection begins abruptly once the incidence angle passes the critical angle predicted by sin θc = 1/n, with denser media (diamond) showing a much smaller critical angle than water or glass.

quiz.question: Bending a concave mirror to a deeper curve (smaller radius of curvature) will:

options.text: Move the focal point farther away
Move the focal point closer to the mirror

quiz.explanation: Since f = R/2, a smaller radius of curvature R produces a shorter focal length f, pulling the focus closer to the mirror.

quiz.question: A candle placed exactly at a convex lens's focal point produces:

options.text: No image — the outgoing rays are parallel

quiz.explanation: At u = f, the lens equation gives v = infinity: every ray leaves the lens parallel to the axis, so no image forms.

quiz.question: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels:

options.text: From a denser medium into a rarer medium, above the critical angle
From a rarer medium into a denser medium, at any angle

quiz.explanation: TIR requires light moving from higher to lower refractive index, and only once the incidence angle exceeds the critical angle sin θc = 1/n.

title: Reverse an Array: In-Place Swap
summary: Master the Two-Pointer technique to reverse an array in-place with O(1) auxiliary space.
theory: Reversing an array or string in-place is a fundamental computer science concept. By using a Left and Right pointer and swapping elements directly, we achieve **O(1) auxiliary space** (no extra memory allocated) and **O(N) time complexity** (linear time).

procedure.title: Initialize Pointers
procedure.description: Drop two markers on the track: L at the first block, R at the last block.

procedure.title: Swap in Place
procedure.description: Swap the block at L with the block at R without allocating a new array.

procedure.title: Move Markers Inward
procedure.description: Slide marker L one step right and marker R one step left, until they meet or cross.

observation: For an 11-letter word, only 5 swaps are needed! Using two pointers is extremely memory efficient compared to creating a duplicate string.

quiz.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of reversing a string in-place using two pointers?
quiz.explanation: We only need memory for two variables (L and R) regardless of the string's length, meaning it requires O(1) constant auxiliary space.

title: Reverse a String: Out-of-Place
summary: Understand why reversing immutable strings requires O(N) extra memory space.
theory: In many programming languages, strings are **immutable**, meaning their characters cannot be modified in-place. To reverse a string without converting it to an array, we must create a completely new string in memory and build it character by character from the end of the original string. This approach results in **O(N) auxiliary space** because we allocate new memory proportional to the string's length.

procedure.title: Allocate New String
procedure.description: Observe how a brand new empty string must be created in memory.

procedure.title: Iterate Backwards
procedure.description: Watch a pointer start at the end of the original string and move backwards.

procedure.title: Concatenate
procedure.description: See each character get appended to the new string, allocating more memory space each time.

observation: Reversing an 11-letter string this way allocates 11 new character slots in memory. Compare this to the Array version, which required 0 extra slots!

quiz.question: Why does reversing an immutable string require O(N) auxiliary space?

options.text: Because it takes N operations to reverse.
Because you must create a new string of length N in memory.
Because strings take up more memory than arrays.
It doesn't, it takes O(1) space.

quiz.explanation: Since the original string cannot be modified, a new string of size N must be built, consuming O(N) extra memory.

title: Palindrome Checker: Two-Pointer Convergence
summary: Use two converging pointers to verify if a string is a palindrome in O(N) time and O(1) space.
theory: A palindrome is a word that reads the same forwards and backwards (e.g., 'racecar'). The most efficient way to check for a palindrome is using the Two-Pointer technique. We place a pointer at the start (L) and end (R) of the string. We compare the characters at these pointers. If they match, we move the pointers inward. If they don't match, it is not a palindrome. We repeat this until the pointers meet in the middle.

procedure.title: Initialize Pointers
procedure.description: Place L at the first character and R at the last character.

procedure.title: Compare Characters
procedure.description: Check if the character at L is identical to the character at R.

procedure.title: Converge
procedure.description: If they match, move L right by 1 and R left by 1. Stop if they don't match.

observation: Notice how the pointers act as a mirror, checking symmetry from the outside in.

quiz.question: What happens the moment the characters at L and R do NOT match?

options.text: The loop continues until they meet.
The function immediately returns False (it is not a palindrome).
The pointers jump back to the start.

quiz.explanation: A single mismatch proves the word is not perfectly symmetrical, so we can stop checking immediately.

title: Potentiometer: Internal Resistance of a Cell
summary: Balance a cell against a potentiometer wire with and without a shunt resistance, then work out the cell's internal resistance from the two balance lengths.
theory: A **potentiometer** is a long wire of uniform cross-section carrying a steady current from a driver cell. Because the wire is uniform, the potential difference across any length l is proportional to l, so the wire has a constant **potential gradient k** (volts per cm). A test cell is connected through a galvanometer to a sliding **jockey**; at the **null point** the galvanometer shows zero deflection, no current flows through the test cell, and the cell's voltage equals k l. **Open circuit (K₂ open):** the balance length l₁ measures the emf, E = k l₁. **Closed circuit (K₂ closed, resistance R across the cell):** a current I = E/(R + r) flows, so the terminal voltage drops to V = E − I r = k l₂. Dividing the two equations gives V/E = l₂/l₁ = R/(R + r), and therefore the internal resistance is **r = R (l₁ − l₂) / l₂**. Plotting (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ against 1/R gives a straight line through the origin whose slope is r. The driver cell's emf must be greater than the test cell's emf, and the positive terminals of both cells must be joined to the same end of the wire.

procedure.title: Check the driver circuit
procedure.description: Leave the rheostat near 2 Ω and read the potential drop across the wire. It must be larger than the cell's emf; if the status bar warns about this, reduce the rheostat resistance.

procedure.title: Find l₁ with K₂ open
procedure.description: Drag the jockey along the wire (use the slider and ±0.1 cm buttons for fine control) until the galvanometer needle sits at zero, then press Record l₁.

procedure.title: Choose a resistance and close K₂
procedure.description: Pick a resistance R from the box (for example 5 Ω) and close key K₂ so that R is connected across the cell.

procedure.title: Find l₂
procedure.description: Slide the jockey to the new null point. It will be shorter than l₁ because the terminal voltage is lower. Press Record l₂.

procedure.title: Repeat for other resistances
procedure.description: Record l₂ for at least four values of R, such as 2, 5, 10 and 20 Ω. Do not change the rheostat, or the potential gradient changes and your readings are cleared.

procedure.title: Calculate r
procedure.description: For each row the table gives (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ and r = R(l₁ − l₂)/l₂. Take the mean of the r values.

procedure.title: Plot the graph and check
procedure.description: Study the graph of (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ against 1/R; its slope is r. Press Check my answer to compare with the cell's actual internal resistance, or try a new unknown cell.

observation: With K₂ open the balance length l₁ is the longest, since it corresponds to the full emf. With K₂ closed the balance length l₂ is always shorter, and it increases towards l₁ as R is made larger because less current is drawn and less voltage is lost across r. The values of r calculated for different R agree closely, and the graph of (l₁ − l₂)/l₂ against 1/R is a straight line through the origin with slope equal to r.

quiz.question: The working principle of a potentiometer is that, for a wire of uniform cross-section carrying a steady current, the potential difference across any length of the wire is:

options.text: Proportional to the square of the length

quiz.explanation: V = I ρ l / A, and with I and A constant the potential difference is directly proportional to the length l.

quiz.question: At the null point the galvanometer shows zero deflection. This means:

options.text: The driver cell has no emf
The jockey is at end A
No current flows through the test cell, so the potentiometer reads its emf

quiz.explanation: At balance the voltage along the wire exactly equals the cell's voltage, so no current is drawn. That is why a potentiometer measures emf accurately where a voltmeter cannot.

quiz.question: With key K₂ closed and a resistance R across the cell, the balance length l₂ compared with l₁ is:
quiz.explanation: When current flows, part of the emf is lost across the internal resistance. The terminal voltage V = E − I r is less than E, so l₂ < l₁.

quiz.question: The internal resistance of the cell is given by:
quiz.explanation: From E = k l₁ and V = k l₂ we get l₂/l₁ = R/(R + r). Rearranging gives r = R (l₁ − l₂)/l₂.

quiz.question: If a larger resistance R is connected across the cell, the balance length l₂ will:
quiz.explanation: A larger R draws less current, so less voltage is lost across r. The terminal voltage approaches E, and l₂ approaches l₁, but it can never exceed it.

quiz.question: No balance point can be found anywhere on the wire. The most likely reason is:

options.text: The potential drop across the wire is less than the emf of the test cell

quiz.explanation: A null point exists only if the voltage across the whole wire exceeds the cell's voltage. Reduce the rheostat resistance, or use a driver cell of higher emf.

quiz.question: Why are the positive terminals of the driver cell and the test cell joined to the same end of the wire?

options.text: To increase the current in the wire
So that the two emfs oppose each other and a null point can be found
To make the potential gradient smaller

quiz.explanation: If the cells were connected the other way round, their emfs would add and the galvanometer could never be brought to zero.

quiz.question: How can the sensitivity of a potentiometer be increased?

options.text: Decrease the potential gradient, using a larger rheostat resistance or a longer wire

quiz.explanation: A smaller potential gradient means a given error in balance length corresponds to a smaller error in voltage, so the measurement is more precise. The wire's total drop must still exceed the cell's emf.

title: Potentiometer: Comparing the EMFs of Two Cells
summary: Balance two cells in turn on a potentiometer wire using a two-way key, and find the ratio of their emfs from the two balance lengths.
theory: A **potentiometer** is a long wire of uniform cross-section carrying a steady current from a driver cell, so the potential difference across any length l of the wire is proportional to l. The wire therefore has a constant **potential gradient k** (volts per cm). A test cell is joined, through a galvanometer, to a sliding **jockey**; at the **null point** the galvanometer shows zero deflection, no current flows through the cell, and its emf equals the potential drop along the balance length. With a **two-way key** the two cells are connected one at a time: for cell E₁ the balance length is l₁, so E₁ = k l₁, and for cell E₂ the balance length is l₂, so E₂ = k l₂. Dividing the equations gives **E₁ / E₂ = l₁ / l₂**, because the gradient k cancels. Changing the rheostat changes k, and therefore both lengths, but not their ratio, so the experiment is repeated for several rheostat settings and the mean ratio is taken. Plotting l₁ against l₂ gives a straight line through the origin whose slope is E₁/E₂. The driver cell's emf must be greater than the emf of either test cell, and the positive terminals of all cells must be joined to the same end of the wire.

procedure.title: Check the driver circuit
procedure.description: Start with the rheostat near 2 Ω and read the potential drop across the wire. It must be larger than the emf of either cell; if the status bar warns about this, reduce the rheostat resistance.

procedure.title: Find l₁ with E₁ connected
procedure.description: Set the two-way key to E₁. Drag the jockey along the wire (use the slider and ±0.1 cm buttons for fine control) until the galvanometer needle sits at zero, then press Record l₁.

procedure.title: Find l₂ with E₂ connected
procedure.description: Without changing the rheostat, switch the two-way key to E₂, find its null point and press Record l₂. The table row for this rheostat setting is now complete.

procedure.title: Read the ratio
procedure.description: The table shows E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂ for the completed set.

procedure.title: Repeat for other rheostat settings
procedure.description: Change the rheostat (for example 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 Ω) and repeat steps 2 and 3, taking at least three sets. Both lengths change with the rheostat, but their ratio should stay almost constant.

procedure.title: Find the mean ratio
procedure.description: Take the mean of E₁/E₂ over all completed sets and write the result.

procedure.title: Plot the graph and check
procedure.description: Study the graph of l₁ against l₂; its slope is E₁/E₂. Press Check my answer to compare with the actual emfs, or try two new unknown cells.

observation: For every rheostat setting the balance length of the cell with the larger emf is longer than that of the other cell. Increasing the rheostat resistance lengthens both balance lengths because the potential gradient falls, but the ratio l₁/l₂ stays nearly constant. The graph of l₁ against l₂ is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals E₁/E₂, in agreement with the mean of the table values.

quiz.question: At the null point with E₁ connected, the potential drop across the balance length l₁ equals:

options.text: The emf of the driver cell

quiz.explanation: At balance no current flows through the cell, so the potential drop k l₁ along the wire exactly equals the emf E₁.

quiz.question: The ratio of the emfs of the two cells is given by:
quiz.explanation: E₁ = k l₁ and E₂ = k l₂, so dividing gives E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂. The gradient k cancels.

quiz.question: A student finds l₁ = 800 cm and l₂ = 500 cm. The ratio E₁/E₂ is:
quiz.explanation: E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂ = 800/500 = 1.6. Note it is a ratio of lengths, so it has no units.

quiz.question: The rheostat resistance is increased and the experiment is repeated. The balance lengths l₁ and l₂ will:

options.text: Both increase, but l₁/l₂ stays the same

quiz.explanation: More rheostat resistance means less current and a smaller potential gradient k, so longer lengths are needed to balance the same emfs. Since k cancels in l₁/l₂, the ratio is unchanged.

quiz.question: No balance point can be found for cell E₁, although one is found for E₂. The most likely reason is:

options.text: The cell E₂ has no internal resistance
The potential drop across the whole wire is smaller than the emf of E₁
The jockey is pressed too hard

quiz.explanation: A null point exists only if the voltage across the entire wire exceeds the cell's emf. E₁ is the larger emf, so reduce the rheostat resistance.

quiz.question: Why is a two-way key used in this experiment?

options.text: To connect either cell to the galvanometer circuit, one at a time, without changing the rest of the circuit
To increase the emf of the driver cell
To reduce the current in the wire
To connect both cells in series

quiz.explanation: The two-way key lets one test cell be balanced and then the other, using the same wire, jockey and galvanometer.

quiz.question: Why must the positive terminals of the driver cell and both test cells be joined to the same end of the wire?

options.text: To make E₁ equal to E₂
So that each test cell opposes the potential drop along the wire and a null point can be found

quiz.explanation: If a test cell were connected the other way round, its emf would add to the wire's potential and the galvanometer could never be brought to zero.

quiz.question: How can the sensitivity of a potentiometer be increased?

options.text: Decrease the potential gradient, using a larger rheostat resistance or a longer wire

quiz.explanation: A smaller potential gradient means a given error in balance length corresponds to a smaller error in voltage. The wire's total drop must still exceed both emfs.

title: Sonometer (3D): Frequency of a Tuning Fork
summary: Use a 3D sonometer to find the resonant lengths of known tuning forks, verify that f × L is constant at fixed tension, and then find the frequency of an unknown fork.
theory: A **sonometer** is a hollow wooden box with a wire stretched along its top between two bridges. The tension comes from weights hung over a pulley. A wire of length L, tension T and mass per unit length μ carries waves at speed **v = √(T/μ)**. When it vibrates in its fundamental mode, the length L is half a wavelength, so its natural frequency is **f = v / 2L = (1/2L)√(T/μ)**. If a tuning fork is sounded and pressed on the box, the wire is forced to vibrate at the fork's frequency. When the length is adjusted until the wire's natural frequency equals the fork's, **resonance** occurs: the wire vibrates with a large amplitude and a small **paper rider** placed on it is thrown off. For a fixed wire and tension, **f × L = v/2 is constant**, so f is proportional to 1/L and a graph of f against 1/L is a straight line through the origin with slope v/2. This allows the unknown frequency of a fork to be found from its resonant length: **f_x = (f × L) / L_x**. The resonant length is proportional to √T for a given fork. The wire must be uniform and taut, the pulley frictionless, and the bridge must be moved slowly near resonance.

procedure.title: Set the tension
procedure.description: Choose the number of slotted weights. The hanger and weights give the tension T = Mg. Keep it the same for the whole experiment, because changing it clears your readings.

procedure.title: Select a known fork
procedure.description: Pick one of the known tuning forks, for example 256 Hz, from the chips and note its frequency.

procedure.title: Strike the fork and place it on the box
procedure.description: Press the strike button. The fork is sounding and its stem is pressed on the box close to the wire. The paper rider sits at the middle of the vibrating length.

procedure.title: Slide the bridge B₂ slowly
procedure.description: Drag B₂ in the 3D view, or use the slider and the 0.1 cm buttons. Watch the rider and the vibration bar. Near resonance the rider trembles, and at resonance it is thrown off the wire.

procedure.title: Record the resonant length
procedure.description: With the rider off, read the length from the scale. The top view shows the reading mark clearly. Press Record. Repeat for the other known forks.

procedure.title: Find the unknown fork
procedure.description: Select Fork X and repeat the procedure at the same tension to find its resonant length L_x.

procedure.title: Calculate and plot
procedure.description: Find f × L for each fork and take the mean. Calculate f_x = (mean f × L) / L_x. Plot f against 1/L and use twice the slope to find the wave speed v. Press Check my answer to compare with the actual values.

observation: The resonant length is shorter for a fork of higher frequency and longer for a larger tension. For every known fork f × L is almost the same, so the graph of f against 1/L is a straight line through the origin. The unknown fork has a frequency f_x = (f × L) / L_x, found from its resonant length. With a tension of about 25 N the wave speed in the wire is about 250 m/s.

quiz.question: The fundamental frequency of a wire of vibrating length L, tension T and mass per unit length μ is:
quiz.explanation: The fundamental mode has a loop in the middle, so L is half a wavelength. With wave speed v = √(T/μ), f = v/λ = v/2L = (1/2L)√(T/μ).

quiz.question: With the tension fixed, the vibrating length of the wire is doubled. Its fundamental frequency becomes:
quiz.explanation: f is proportional to 1/L when T and μ are fixed, so doubling L halves f.

quiz.question: With the wire and tension unchanged, which quantity stays constant for forks of different frequency?
quiz.explanation: Because f = v/2L, the product f × L = v/2 is the same for every fork, as long as the tension does not change.

quiz.question: The paper rider is thrown off the wire when:

options.text: The length of the wire equals one full wavelength
The natural frequency of the wire equals the frequency of the fork
The tension in the wire becomes zero

quiz.explanation: At resonance the wire vibrates with a large amplitude, which throws off the paper rider.

quiz.question: A 256 Hz fork resonates at L = 50 cm. An unknown fork resonates at L = 40 cm under the same tension. Its frequency is:
quiz.explanation: f × L is constant, so f = 256 × 50 / 40 = 320 Hz.

quiz.question: A graph of frequency f against 1/L for a wire at fixed tension is a straight line through the origin. Its slope equals:
quiz.explanation: f = (v/2)(1/L), so the slope of f against 1/L is v/2 and the wave speed is v = 2 × slope.

quiz.question: For the same fork, the tension in the wire is made four times larger. The resonant length becomes:
quiz.explanation: L = (1/2f)√(T/μ), so L is proportional to √T. Four times the tension gives twice the length.

quiz.question: The sonometer wire is stretched over a hollow wooden box because the box:

options.text: Acts as a sounding board that makes the wire vibrate strongly
Reduces the tension in the wire
Insulates the wire from the fork

quiz.explanation: The hollow box is a sounding board. It takes up the vibrations of the fork and passes them to the wire, and it makes the sound of the vibrating wire louder.

title: Meter Bridge: Resistance and Resistivity of a Wire
summary: Balance a known resistance against an unknown wire on a metre-long bridge wire, find the unknown resistance from the null point, and calculate the resistivity of the wire.
theory: A **meter bridge** is a practical form of the **Wheatstone bridge**. A uniform wire AB of length 100 cm is stretched along a metre scale and joined to two gaps by thick copper strips. A known resistance **R** from a resistance box is placed in one gap and the unknown wire **X** in the other. A galvanometer is connected between the middle point D of the strips and a sliding **jockey** on the wire. A cell and a key send current through AB. When the jockey touches the wire at the **null point**, at a distance l from A, the galvanometer shows no deflection and the bridge is balanced. The resistance of each part of the uniform wire is proportional to its length, so **R / X = l / (100 − l)**, which gives **X = R (100 − l) / l**. The reading is repeated for several values of R and the mean of X is taken. A graph of l / (100 − l) against R is a straight line through the origin with slope 1/X. If the length L and the diameter d of the unknown wire are known, its **resistivity** is **ρ = X A / L = X π d² / 4L**. The balance point should lie near the middle of the wire, where the percentage error is smallest. The key must be kept closed only while taking a reading, so that the heating of the wire does not change its resistance.

procedure.title: Note the wire details
procedure.description: Read the length L and the diameter d of the unknown wire from the card. In the laboratory d is measured with a screw gauge at several places.

procedure.title: Choose a resistance R
procedure.description: Pick a value of R from the resistance box. Start with about 5 Ω; a value close to the unknown resistance puts the balance point near the middle of the wire.

procedure.title: Find the null point
procedure.description: Drag the jockey along the wire, then use the slider and the 0.1 cm buttons until the galvanometer needle is at zero and the ring turns green.

procedure.title: Record l
procedure.description: Press Record. The table gives l, 100 − l and X = R(100 − l)/l. If the balance point is near an end of the wire, choose a different R.

procedure.title: Repeat for other values of R
procedure.description: Take at least four readings with different R, keeping the balance points between about 30 cm and 70 cm.

procedure.title: Find the mean and the graph
procedure.description: Read the mean X from the table. Check it with the graph of l/(100 − l) against R, whose slope is 1/X.

procedure.title: Calculate the resistivity
procedure.description: Use ρ = X π d² / 4L with the mean X. Press Check my answer to compare X and ρ with the actual values and see which material the wire is made of.

observation: The balance length l increases as R is increased, because a larger R needs a longer part of the wire to balance. For every reading the value of X = R(100 − l)/l is nearly the same, and the graph of l/(100 − l) against R is a straight line through the origin. The mean X and the dimensions of the wire give its resistivity, which agrees with a standard value for materials such as constantan, manganin and nichrome.

quiz.question: In a meter bridge, R is in the left gap and the unknown X in the right gap. If the balance length from the left end is l cm, then X equals:
quiz.explanation: At balance R / X = l / (100 − l), because the resistance of each part of the uniform wire is proportional to its length. So X = R (100 − l) / l.

quiz.question: The balance point should be near the middle of the wire (about 50 cm) because then:

options.text: The percentage error in X is smallest

quiz.explanation: The error in X caused by a given error in l is smallest when l is near 50 cm. Near the ends the same reading error produces a much larger error in X.

quiz.question: A meter bridge works on the principle of the:
quiz.explanation: The two gaps and the two parts of the wire form the four arms of a Wheatstone bridge, balanced when the galvanometer shows zero.

quiz.question: With R = 6 Ω the null point is at l = 40 cm. The unknown resistance X is:
After one reading, R and X are interchanged and the reading is repeated. This is done to:

options.text: Remove the error due to the end resistances of the bridge
Increase the current in the wire

quiz.explanation: The copper strips and connections add small resistances at the ends. Interchanging R and X and taking the mean cancels this error.

quiz.question: The resistivity of the material of the unknown wire, of length L and diameter d, is:
quiz.explanation: ρ = X A / L and the area of cross-section is A = π d² / 4, so ρ = X π d² / 4L.

quiz.question: The key is kept closed only while a reading is taken because:

options.text: The current heats the wire and changes its resistance
The galvanometer would be damaged by a small current
The wire would expand and become longer

quiz.explanation: A steady current heats the wire. Its resistance then rises with temperature and the readings are no longer for the original resistance.

quiz.question: If the diameter of a wire is doubled, with the length and material unchanged, its resistance becomes:
quiz.explanation: R = ρL/A and A is proportional to d². Doubling d makes A four times larger, so R falls to one quarter.

title: Ohm's Law: V–I Graph, Series and Parallel Resistances
summary: Vary the current with a rheostat, read a voltmeter and an ammeter, find an unknown resistance from the V–I graph, and verify the laws for resistors in series and in parallel.
theory: **Ohm's law** states that, at constant temperature, the current I through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference V across its ends, so **V = I R**. The constant R is the **resistance** of the conductor, and the graph of V against I is a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. In the experiment a cell, a key, a rheostat and an **ammeter** are connected in series with the resistor, and a **voltmeter** is connected in parallel across it. The rheostat changes the current, and for each setting V and I are read. The ratio V / I is calculated for every reading and the mean is taken, which is checked against the slope of the graph. For two resistors in **series** the same current flows through both and the total resistance is **R_s = R₁ + R₂**. For two resistors in **parallel** the same potential difference is across both, and **1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂**, so R_p = R₁R₂ / (R₁ + R₂), which is smaller than either resistance. The key is kept closed only while taking a reading, so that heating does not change the resistance. A real voltmeter draws a small current, so the value of V / I is very slightly smaller than the true resistance.

procedure.title: Connect R₁ alone
procedure.description: Select R₁. The circuit shows the cell, key, rheostat, ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the resistor.

procedure.title: Set the rheostat and take a reading
procedure.description: Move the rheostat to a setting and press Take reading. The ammeter and voltmeter values are entered in the table with V / I.

procedure.title: Repeat for at least five settings
procedure.description: Change the rheostat to vary the current over a wide range. Keep the current below about 2 A so that the resistor does not heat up.

procedure.title: Find R₁ from the table and the graph
procedure.description: Read the mean V / I. Check it against the slope of the V–I graph, which is a straight line through the origin.

procedure.title: Repeat for R₂
procedure.description: Select R₂ and repeat the readings to find its resistance.

procedure.title: Series and parallel
procedure.description: Select Series and then Parallel and take readings for each. Compare the measured resistance with R₁ + R₂ and with R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) in the summary table.

procedure.title: Check your answer
procedure.description: Press Check my answer to see the actual resistances and your percentage errors. Press New resistors to practise with different values.

observation: For each resistor, V / I is nearly the same for every rheostat setting, so the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin. The measured resistance of the series combination is close to R₁ + R₂ and is larger than either resistor. The measured resistance of the parallel combination is close to R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) and is smaller than either resistor.

quiz.question: For a conductor obeying Ohm's law, the graph of potential difference V against current I is:

options.text: A straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the I axis
A straight line with a negative slope

quiz.explanation: Ohm's law says V is proportional to I at constant temperature, so V–I is a straight line through the origin.

quiz.question: The slope of the V–I graph of a resistor gives its:
quiz.explanation: V = I R, so the slope of V against I is the resistance R.

quiz.question: The ammeter and the voltmeter are connected, respectively:
quiz.explanation: The ammeter must carry the whole current, so it is in series. The voltmeter measures the potential difference across the resistor, so it is in parallel with it.

quiz.question: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in series. The equivalent resistance is:
Two resistors of 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:
The equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel is always:

options.text: Equal to the sum of the two
Equal to the mean of the two

quiz.explanation: Each branch gives the current an extra path, so the combination conducts more easily than either resistor alone.

quiz.question: The key is kept closed only while taking a reading because:

options.text: The current heats the resistor and changes its resistance

quiz.explanation: Heating raises the temperature of the resistor, so Ohm's law no longer holds with a constant R.

quiz.question: A real voltmeter has a very large but finite resistance. The measured value of V / I for a resistor is therefore:
quiz.explanation: The voltmeter takes a small current, so the ammeter reads slightly more than the current in the resistor. V / I is then slightly less than R.

title: Convex Lens (3D): Focal Length by the u–v Method
summary: Use a 3D optical bench to place a lit object at different distances from a convex lens, find the sharp image on a screen, and calculate the focal length from u and v, with a u–v graph and a 1/u–1/v graph.
theory: A **convex lens** converges parallel rays to its **principal focus**, at a distance f called the **focal length**. If a luminous object is placed beyond the focal length, the rays from each point meet again on the other side and form a **real, inverted image** that can be caught on a screen. With the object at a distance u from the lens and the sharp image at a distance v, the **lens formula** applies: with the Cartesian sign convention **1/v − 1/u = 1/f**, and in magnitudes **1/u + 1/v = 1/f**, so **f = uv / (u + v)**. The linear magnification is **m = v / u**. For u = 2f the image is formed at v = 2f and is the same size as the object. For u < f no real image is formed. In the experiment the lens is fixed on the optical bench, the object is placed at a chosen distance u, and the screen is moved until the image is sharp, which gives v. The readings are repeated for several values of u and the mean f is found. A graph of v against u is a smooth curve. A graph of 1/v against 1/u is a straight line whose intercept on either axis is 1/f. The image is difficult to focus when u is close to f or when it is very large, so values of u between 1.5 f and 3 f are best. The lens, object and screen should be at the same height with their centres on the optical axis.

procedure.title: Set up the bench
procedure.description: The lens is fixed at the 40 cm mark of the optical bench. The lit object and the screen slide along the bench on either side. Use the overview or the side view to see the arrangement.

procedure.title: Choose an object distance u
procedure.description: Set u with the slider, or drag the object along the bench. Try values between about 1.5 f and 3 f. If you do not know f yet, start with u about 25 to 35 cm.

procedure.title: Find the sharp image
procedure.description: Move the screen with the slider, the 0.1 cm buttons or by dragging it. The rays in the 3D view meet at a point when the image is in focus, and the sharpness bar fills up.

procedure.title: Record u and v
procedure.description: When the image is sharp, check it by moving the screen a little each side, then press Record. The table gives f = uv/(u + v) and 1/u, 1/v.

procedure.title: Repeat for several values of u
procedure.description: Take at least five readings for different u. If the image falls beyond the end of the bench, increase u.

procedure.title: Find f from the table and the graphs
procedure.description: Read the mean f. The graph of 1/v against 1/u should be a straight line, and its intercept on the 1/v axis is 1/f.

procedure.title: Check your answer
procedure.description: Press Check my answer to see the actual focal length and your percentage error, and the power of the lens in dioptres. Press New unknown lens to try a lens with a different focal length.

observation: The sharp image on the screen is real and inverted. As u is decreased towards 2f the image moves away from the lens and grows larger, and for u between f and 2f it is larger than the object. The value of f = uv/(u + v) is nearly the same for every pair of readings. The graph of v against u is a smooth curve and the graph of 1/v against 1/u is a straight line with a slope close to −1 and equal intercepts on the two axes.

quiz.question: For a thin convex lens, with u and v taken as magnitudes for a real image, the focal length is:
quiz.explanation: With magnitudes the lens formula is 1/u + 1/v = 1/f, which gives f = uv / (u + v).

quiz.question: When a convex lens of focal length f forms a real image of an object placed at u = 2f, the image is formed at:

options.text: v = 2f, inverted and the same size as the object
v = 2f, upright and the same size

quiz.explanation: 1/v = 1/f − 1/(2f) = 1/(2f), so v = 2f. The magnification is v/u = 1, and the real image is inverted.

quiz.question: A graph of 1/v against 1/u for a convex lens is a straight line. Its intercept on the 1/v axis is:
quiz.explanation: With magnitudes 1/u + 1/v = 1/f, so 1/v = 1/f − 1/u. When 1/u = 0 the value of 1/v equals 1/f, which is the intercept on the 1/v axis.

quiz.question: With u = 30 cm, the sharp image on the screen is at v = 30 cm. The focal length is:
If the object is placed closer to the lens than its focal length (u < f), then:

options.text: A sharp inverted image forms on a distant screen
The image is formed at the focus
No real image can be obtained on the screen

quiz.explanation: For u < f the rays leave the lens still diverging, so they do not meet. The image is virtual, erect and magnified, and cannot be caught on a screen.

quiz.question: The linear magnification produced by the lens is:
quiz.explanation: The magnitude of the magnification is the ratio of the image distance to the object distance, m = v / u.

quiz.question: With the Cartesian sign convention, the object distance u for a real object placed to the left of the lens is:
quiz.explanation: Distances are measured from the lens, positive in the direction of the incident light. An object on the left therefore has a negative u.

quiz.question: For a more accurate value of f, readings are taken with u between about 1.5 f and 3 f. This is because:

options.text: The image is then magnified the most
Very near f the image distance is huge and hard to measure
The lens then has no aberrations at all

quiz.explanation: Near u = f the image goes far away and its position is hard to find precisely. For large u the image is tiny and v is almost f, so the readings are less informative.

title: Prism (3D): Angle of Minimum Deviation and Refractive Index
summary: Turn a 60° glass prism on a drawing board in 3D, read the deviation of the emergent ray on a protractor, plot the i–δ curve, find the minimum deviation and calculate the refractive index.
theory:
When a ray of light passes through a prism it bends towards the base, and the angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray is the **angle of deviation δ**. For a prism of angle A, **δ = i + e − A**, where i is the angle of incidence and e the angle of emergence.

As i is increased, δ first decreases, reaches a **minimum deviation D**, and then increases again. At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism: **i = e** and **r₁ = r₂ = A/2**, and the ray inside is parallel to the base.

Applying Snell's law at the first face with i = (A + D)/2 and r = A/2 gives the **refractive index n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2)**. For A = 60° this becomes n = sin(30° + D/2) / sin 30°.

procedure.title: Set up the prism
procedure.description: Place the prism on the drawing board with its refracting edge upright. The prism angle is A = 60°. A narrow beam from the light source falls on the first face at the point marked M₁.

procedure.title: Choose the angle of incidence
procedure.description: Turn the prism with the slider or by dragging it. Start at about i = 35° and increase in steps of about 5°.

procedure.title: Read the deviation
procedure.description: Read δ on the protractor where the emergent ray crosses the scale. This is the angle between the emergent ray and the straight-on direction of the incident ray.

procedure.title: Record readings
procedure.description: Press Record i and δ. Take at least ten readings, with smaller steps near the lowest δ where the emergent ray hardly moves.

procedure.title: Find the minimum
procedure.description: Study the i–δ graph. The lowest point of the smooth curve gives the minimum deviation D and the angle of incidence at which i = e.

procedure.title: Calculate n
procedure.description: Use n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2). Press New unknown prism and repeat to practise with a different glass.

observation: Angle of the prism A = 60°. Record i and δ for about ten angles of incidence from 35° to 70°. The graph of δ against i is a U-shaped curve. The minimum deviation D is read at its lowest point, and n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2). Typical glass gives n between 1.48 and 1.66.

quiz.question: A ray passes through a prism. The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray is called the:
quiz.explanation: The angle through which the ray is turned from its original direction is the angle of deviation δ.

quiz.question: When the angle of incidence i is increased from a small value, the deviation δ:

options.text: First decreases to a minimum, then increases

quiz.explanation: The i–δ curve is U-shaped: δ falls, reaches the minimum deviation D, and then rises.

quiz.question: At the position of minimum deviation:

options.text: i = r₁ and e = r₂ only

quiz.explanation: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically, so the angle of emergence equals the angle of incidence and r₁ = r₂ = A/2.

quiz.question: At minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism is:

options.text: Along the normal to the second face

quiz.explanation: Since r₁ = r₂ the ray inside makes equal angles with both faces, so it runs parallel to the base.

quiz.question: The refractive index of the prism material in terms of the prism angle A and the minimum deviation D is:
quiz.explanation: Putting i = (A + D)/2 and r = A/2 in Snell's law gives n = sin((A + D)/2) / sin(A/2).

quiz.question: For a prism of angle 60° the minimum deviation is 37°. The refractive index is nearly:
If the angle of incidence is made too small, the ray may not emerge from the second face. This is due to:
quiz.explanation: Inside the glass the ray meets the second face at more than the critical angle, so it is totally reflected.

quiz.question: Why are several readings taken near the lowest point of the i–δ graph, and a smooth curve drawn through them?

options.text: The curve is flat there, so the minimum is found more reliably from the smooth curve than from one reading
The ray becomes parallel to the normal there

quiz.explanation: Near the minimum δ changes very little with i, so single readings are close together; the lowest point of the smooth curve gives D reliably.

title: p-n Junction Diode: Forward and Reverse Bias Characteristics
summary: Plot the I–V characteristic of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias, find the knee voltage and the forward and reverse resistances, and decide whether the diode is silicon or germanium.
theory:
A **p-n junction** has a thin depletion layer with a potential barrier. In **forward bias** (p side to the positive terminal) the barrier is lowered. Almost no current flows until the applied voltage reaches the **knee (cut-in) voltage**, about **0.7 V for silicon** and **0.3 V for germanium**; beyond it the current rises steeply.

In **reverse bias** (n side to the positive terminal) the barrier and the depletion layer grow. Only a very small **reverse saturation current** of minority carriers flows: nanoamperes for silicon and microamperes for germanium.

The **forward (dynamic) resistance r_f = ΔV/ΔI** is measured on the steep part of the forward curve and is a few ohms. The **reverse resistance r_r = ΔV/ΔI** on the reverse curve is of the order of megaohms. The knee voltage is found by extending the straight, steep part of the forward curve to meet the voltage axis.

procedure.title: Connect in forward bias
procedure.description: Join the p side of the diode to the positive terminal through the rheostat, a 100 Ω protective resistor and a milliammeter. Connect the voltmeter across the diode.

procedure.title: Take forward readings
procedure.description: Raise the supply from zero in small steps and record the voltage V across the diode and the current I in mA. Take closer readings near the knee, up to about 25 mA.

procedure.title: Connect in reverse bias
procedure.description: Switch to reverse bias: the n side goes to the positive terminal and the milliammeter is replaced by a microammeter.

procedure.title: Take reverse readings
procedure.description: Increase the reverse voltage in steps of 2 V up to 20 V and record the reverse current in µA.

procedure.title: Draw the characteristic
procedure.description: Plot forward readings in the first quadrant (mA) and reverse readings in the third quadrant (µA) with different scales.

procedure.title: Find the results
procedure.description: Extend the steep part of the forward curve to the V axis for the knee voltage. Find r_f and r_r from ΔV/ΔI. Use the knee voltage to decide whether the diode is silicon or germanium.

observation: Record V (V) and I (mA) in forward bias and V (V) and I (µA) in reverse bias. The forward current stays almost zero up to the knee and then rises steeply; the reverse current is tiny and grows slowly. Knee voltage about 0.7 V (Si) or 0.3 V (Ge); r_f a few ohms; r_r of the order of megaohms.

quiz.question: In forward bias, the p side of the diode is connected to:

options.text: The negative terminal of the battery
The positive terminal of the battery

quiz.explanation: Forward bias means the p side is at a higher potential, so it is joined to the positive terminal.

quiz.question: The knee voltage of a silicon diode is about:
quiz.explanation: Silicon has a barrier potential of about 0.7 V; germanium about 0.3 V.

quiz.question: Why is a protective resistor used in the forward bias circuit?

options.text: To limit the current and protect the diode
To make the diode conduct in reverse

quiz.explanation: Beyond the knee the current rises very steeply; the series resistor limits it to a safe value.

quiz.question: In reverse bias, a microammeter is used instead of a milliammeter because:

options.text: The reverse current is very large
The reverse current is very small (µA or less)

quiz.explanation: Only a tiny reverse saturation current of minority carriers flows, which a milliammeter cannot read.

quiz.question: The forward (dynamic) resistance of a diode is found from:

options.text: ΔV/ΔI on the steep part of the forward curve
The knee voltage divided by 1 mA

quiz.explanation: r_f = ΔV/ΔI is the reciprocal of the slope of the steep, nearly straight part of the forward characteristic.

quiz.question: Compared with the forward resistance, the reverse resistance of a diode is:
quiz.explanation: A diode conducts easily in one direction only: r_f is a few ohms while r_r is of the order of megaohms.

quiz.question: In reverse bias, the width of the depletion layer:
quiz.explanation: The reverse voltage pulls the majority carriers away from the junction, widening the depletion layer and raising the barrier.

quiz.question: A diode has a knee voltage of 0.29 V and a reverse current of about 20 µA at 10 V. It is most likely made of:
quiz.explanation: A low knee voltage (about 0.3 V) and a reverse current of microamperes are typical of germanium.

title: Concave Mirror (3D): Focal Length by the u–v Method
summary: Set up a lit object, a concave mirror and a screen on a 3D optical bench, focus the inverted real image for several object distances, and find the focal length from f = uv/(u + v) and the 1/u–1/v graph.
theory:
A **concave mirror** converges light. When an object is placed beyond its focus, a **real, inverted image** forms in front of the mirror and can be caught on a screen placed on the same side as the object.

The distances are related by the **mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f**. With the Cartesian sign convention u, v and f are all negative for a real image, so in magnitudes **f = uv/(u + v)**. The **radius of curvature is R = 2f**.

When the object is at the **centre of curvature (u = 2f)** the image also forms there, so u = v = 2f. A graph of v against u is a rectangular hyperbola, and a graph of **1/v against 1/u is a straight line** cutting both axes at 1/f.

procedure.title: Find a rough focal length
procedure.description: Focus the image of a distant object on the screen. The distance from the mirror to the screen is roughly f. Here the hidden mirror has f between 10 and 20 cm.

procedure.title: Place the object
procedure.description: Set the object at a distance u from the mirror, beyond the focus. Start at about 1.5 f.

procedure.title: Focus the image
procedure.description: Slide the screen until the inverted image of the arrow is sharpest. Move it a little either side and settle on the middle of the sharp range.

procedure.title: Record u and v
procedure.description: Read u and v on the bench scale and press Record u and v. The table works out f = uv/(u + v).

procedure.title: Repeat
procedure.description: Repeat for at least five values of u between 1.5 f and 3 f, including one where u and v are nearly equal.

procedure.title: Graphs and result
procedure.description: Find the mean f. Plot v against u and 1/v against 1/u; the intercepts of the straight line give 1/f. Then R = 2f.

observation: For each object distance u, record the image distance v at best focus, and calculate f = uv/(u + v). The values of f agree closely; their mean is the focal length. The 1/v–1/u graph is a straight line with slope about −1 and intercept 1/f on both axes. R = 2f.

quiz.question: For a concave mirror, the mirror formula is:
quiz.explanation: For mirrors, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, with all distances measured from the pole using the sign convention.

quiz.question: A concave mirror forms a real image on a screen only when the object is:

options.text: Between the pole and the focus

quiz.explanation: If the object is inside the focal length the reflected rays diverge, and only a virtual image forms behind the mirror.

quiz.question: When the object is at the centre of curvature, the image is formed:

options.text: At the centre of curvature itself

quiz.explanation: With u = 2f the mirror formula gives v = 2f, so object and image coincide in position at C.

quiz.question: The radius of curvature R of a spherical mirror is related to its focal length f by:
quiz.explanation: For a spherical mirror of small aperture, f = R/2.

quiz.question: In the u–v method for a concave mirror, the real image on the screen is:
quiz.explanation: A real image formed by a concave mirror is always inverted. It can be larger or smaller than the object.

quiz.question: A student records u = 30 cm and v = 20 cm for a concave mirror. The focal length is:
With the Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a concave mirror is:
quiz.explanation: The focus of a concave mirror lies in front of it, against the direction of the incident light, so f is negative.

quiz.question: A quick way to find the rough focal length of a concave mirror before the experiment is to:

options.text: Measure the diameter of the mirror
Use the mirror to view your face closely
Focus the image of a distant object, such as a window, on a screen

quiz.explanation: Rays from a distant object are nearly parallel, so their image forms at the focus; the mirror-to-screen distance is then about f.

title: Zener Diode: I–V Characteristic and Reverse Breakdown Voltage
summary: Draw the forward and reverse characteristics of a Zener diode, find its breakdown (Zener) voltage from the graph, and see how it holds the voltage steady as a voltage regulator.
theory:
A **Zener diode** is a heavily doped p-n junction designed to work in **reverse breakdown**. In **forward bias** it behaves like an ordinary silicon diode, with a knee near **0.7 V**.

In **reverse bias** only a tiny current flows until the reverse voltage reaches the **Zener voltage V_Z**. Because heavy doping makes the depletion layer very thin, the electric field there is strong enough to break covalent bonds (**Zener breakdown**), and the reverse current rises sharply.

Beyond breakdown the **voltage across the diode stays almost constant at V_Z** over a wide range of current. Any extra supply voltage appears across the **series resistor**, which also limits the current: **V_supply = V_Z + I R**. This makes the Zener diode a **voltage regulator**. The small **dynamic resistance r_Z = ΔV/ΔI** after breakdown measures how well it regulates.

procedure.title: Forward bias
procedure.description: Connect the p side to the positive terminal through the 220 Ω series resistor and a milliammeter, with a voltmeter across the Zener diode.

procedure.title: Take forward readings
procedure.description: Raise the supply from zero up to 5 V and record V and I. Note the knee near 0.7 V.

procedure.title: Reverse bias
procedure.description: Switch to reverse bias so that the n side (the banded end) goes to the positive terminal.

procedure.title: Take reverse readings
procedure.description: Raise the supply in small steps up to 12 V. Record V and I, taking closer readings where the current begins to rise sharply.

procedure.title: Notice the regulation
procedure.description: After breakdown, see that the voltage across the Zener hardly changes while the current keeps increasing.

procedure.title: Draw the curve and find V_Z
procedure.description: Plot forward readings in the first quadrant and reverse readings in the third. Extend the steep breakdown part to the V axis to get V_Z, and compare it with standard ratings.

observation: In reverse bias the current is nearly zero until the breakdown voltage and then rises steeply, while the voltage stays almost constant. The Zener voltage V_Z is read where the steep part meets the voltage axis. The forward characteristic shows a knee at about 0.7 V.

quiz.question: A Zener diode is normally operated in:

options.text: Reverse bias beyond the breakdown voltage
Reverse bias below the breakdown voltage

quiz.explanation: A Zener is designed to work in the reverse breakdown region, where its voltage stays nearly constant.

quiz.question: After breakdown, as the reverse current through a Zener diode increases, the voltage across it:
quiz.explanation: In breakdown the voltage stays almost equal to V_Z over a wide range of current. This is the basis of voltage regulation.

quiz.question: Zener breakdown occurs in a heavily doped junction because:

options.text: The thin depletion layer has a very strong electric field

quiz.explanation: Heavy doping makes the depletion layer thin, so even a few volts give a field strong enough to pull electrons out of covalent bonds.

quiz.question: Why is a resistor connected in series with a Zener diode in the circuit?

options.text: To make the diode conduct in forward bias
To limit the current after breakdown

quiz.explanation: Beyond breakdown the diode voltage stays near V_Z, so without a series resistor the current could rise enough to destroy it.

quiz.question: In the Zener circuit, the supply is 10 V, V_Z = 6.2 V and the series resistance is 220 Ω. The current is about:
In forward bias, a silicon Zener diode:

options.text: Conducts like an ordinary diode after about 0.7 V
Conducts at any voltage with a constant current

quiz.explanation: In forward bias a Zener behaves like an ordinary silicon diode, with a knee near 0.7 V.

quiz.question: The breakdown voltage V_Z is found from the characteristic by:

options.text: Extending the steep reverse breakdown part of the curve to the voltage axis

quiz.explanation: The nearly vertical breakdown part, extended to meet the V axis, gives V_Z.

quiz.question: A common use of a Zener diode is as a:
quiz.explanation: Because its voltage stays nearly constant in breakdown, a Zener keeps the output voltage steady when the input or load changes.

title: Glass Slab (3D): Refractive Index with a Travelling Microscope
summary: Focus a 3D travelling microscope on a mark, on its image through a glass slab and on powder on the slab, read the vernier yourself, and find n = real thickness / apparent thickness.
theory:
A mark seen through a glass slab looks **raised**, because rays leaving the glass bend **away from the normal**. For near-normal viewing the **apparent thickness is t/n**, where t is the real thickness and n the refractive index, so the mark appears raised by **t(1 − 1/n)**.

A **travelling microscope** moves up and down on a vertical scale with a vernier. Its **least count** is 1 main scale division / number of vernier divisions; here **0.05 cm / 50 = 0.001 cm**. A reading is the **main scale reading** plus the **vernier coincidence × least count**.

Focus on the mark (**R₁**), place the slab and focus on the image of the mark (**R₂**), then sprinkle powder on top and focus on it (**R₃**). The **real thickness is R₃ − R₁**, the **apparent thickness is R₃ − R₂**, and **n = (R₃ − R₁)/(R₃ − R₂)**.

procedure.title: Find the least count
procedure.description: Note the value of one main scale division (0.05 cm) and the number of vernier divisions (50). Least count = 0.05/50 = 0.001 cm.

procedure.title: Focus on the mark (R₁)
procedure.description: Lower the microscope until the cross mark on the paper is sharp. Read the main scale and the vernier coincidence and record R₁.

procedure.title: Place the slab (R₂)
procedure.description: Put the glass slab on the mark. The mark goes out of focus. Raise the microscope until the image of the mark is sharp again and record R₂.

procedure.title: Sprinkle powder (R₃)
procedure.description: Sprinkle a little powder on top of the slab. Raise the microscope until the powder is sharp and record R₃.

procedure.title: Repeat with other slabs
procedure.description: Repeat for the three slabs of different thickness. For each, real thickness = R₃ − R₁ and apparent thickness = R₃ − R₂.

procedure.title: Calculate and plot
procedure.description: Find n = (R₃ − R₁)/(R₃ − R₂) for each slab and take the mean. Plot real against apparent thickness: the slope is n.

observation: For each slab record R₁, R₂ and R₃ using MSR + VSC × 0.001 cm. Real thickness = R₃ − R₁, apparent thickness = R₃ − R₂, n = real/apparent. The values of n agree, and the real–apparent graph is a straight line through the origin with slope n (about 1.5 for glass).

quiz.question: A mark under a glass slab appears raised because light from it:

options.text: Bends away from the normal as it leaves the glass
Bends towards the normal as it leaves the glass

quiz.explanation: On passing from glass to air the rays bend away from the normal, so they seem to come from a point above the real mark.

quiz.question: With a travelling microscope, the refractive index of the slab is:
quiz.explanation: n = real thickness / apparent thickness = (R₃ − R₁)/(R₃ − R₂).

quiz.question: A travelling microscope has a main scale division of 0.05 cm and 50 vernier divisions. Its least count is:
quiz.explanation: LC = 1 MSD / number of vernier divisions = 0.05/50 = 0.001 cm.

quiz.question: The main scale reading is 3.20 cm and the 18th vernier division coincides. With LC = 0.001 cm the reading is:
quiz.explanation: Reading = MSR + VSC × LC = 3.20 + 18 × 0.001 = 3.218 cm.

quiz.question: Why is fine powder sprinkled on the top of the slab?

options.text: So the microscope has something to focus on at the top surface
To remove parallax from the mark

quiz.explanation: A clean glass surface cannot be focused on; the powder particles mark the top surface, giving R₃.

quiz.question: A slab of real thickness 3.0 cm has refractive index 1.5. The mark under it appears raised by:
quiz.explanation: Apparent thickness = 3.0/1.5 = 2.0 cm, so the mark is raised by 3.0 − 2.0 = 1.0 cm = t(1 − 1/n).

quiz.question: Why is the microscope moved in one direction only while focusing?

options.text: To avoid backlash error in the screw

quiz.explanation: Reversing direction lets the screw slip a little before the carriage moves (backlash), which shifts the reading.

quiz.question: A graph of real thickness against apparent thickness for slabs of the same glass is:

options.text: A straight line through the origin with slope 1/n
A straight line through the origin with slope n

quiz.explanation: Real = n × apparent, so the graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope is n.

title: Galvanometer: Resistance by Half Deflection and Figure of Merit
summary: Pass a small current through a galvanometer with a high resistance, then shunt it until the deflection halves. Find its resistance G = RS/(R − S) and its figure of merit k = E/((R + G)θ).
theory:
A **galvanometer** gives a deflection θ proportional to the current through it. The **figure of merit k** is the current needed for one division, **k = I/θ**.

With a high resistance **R** in series and the shunt key open, the current is **I = E/(R + G)**, so **k = E/((R + G)θ)**.

Next a **shunt S** is connected across the galvanometer and adjusted, with R unchanged, until the deflection falls to **θ/2**. Solving the circuit gives the **galvanometer resistance G = RS/(R − S)**. Because R ≫ S, **G ≈ S**.

procedure.title: Set a high resistance
procedure.description: Set the resistance box R to a few thousand ohms before closing the main key K₁, to protect the galvanometer.

procedure.title: Record θ
procedure.description: With K₂ open, adjust R until the deflection is large (20–30 div, preferably even) and record θ.

procedure.title: Close the shunt key
procedure.description: Close K₂. Without changing R, adjust the shunt S until the deflection is exactly θ/2. Record S.

procedure.title: Calculate G and k
procedure.description: Calculate G = RS/(R − S) and k = E/((R + G)θ) with E = 2 V.

procedure.title: Repeat
procedure.description: Open K₂, choose another value of R and repeat. Take at least four sets and find the mean G and mean k.

observation: For each R record θ (K₂ open) and the S that gives θ/2 (K₂ closed). G = RS/(R − S) is nearly equal to S and is the same for every set. The figure of merit k = E/((R + G)θ) is of the order of 10⁻⁵ A per division.

quiz.question: In the half-deflection method, the galvanometer resistance is given by:
quiz.explanation: When the shunt S halves the deflection with R unchanged, solving the circuit gives G = RS/(R − S).

quiz.question: Why is G approximately equal to S in this experiment?

options.text: Because R is much larger than S
Because the battery has no resistance
Because S is larger than R

quiz.explanation: G = RS/(R − S) ≈ S when R ≫ S, since R/(R − S) is then very close to 1.

quiz.question: The figure of merit of a galvanometer is:

options.text: The number of divisions per ampere
The current needed for a deflection of one division
The maximum current it can carry

quiz.explanation: Figure of merit k is the current that produces one division of deflection, k = I/θ.

quiz.question: With E = 2 V, R = 4950 Ω, G = 50 Ω and θ = 20 div, the figure of merit is:
Why must R be set to a high value before closing the main key?

options.text: To protect the galvanometer from a large current
To reduce the emf of the cell

quiz.explanation: A galvanometer is very sensitive; without a large series resistance the current would be large enough to damage it.

quiz.question: While adjusting S for half deflection, the value of R must:
quiz.explanation: The formula assumes the same R in both steps, so R must not be changed while S is adjusted.

quiz.question: If the deflection with the shunt is more than θ/2, you should:
quiz.explanation: A smaller shunt resistance takes more current away from the galvanometer, so its deflection falls.

quiz.question: Why is R chosen so that θ is large and even?

options.text: So θ/2 is a whole number and reading errors are a small fraction

quiz.explanation: A large deflection reduces the percentage error, and an even θ makes θ/2 easy to read.

title: Liquid Lens (3D): Refractive Index of a Liquid using a Convex Lens and a Plane Mirror
summary: Find the focal length of a convex lens on a plane mirror by removing parallax, repeat with liquid under the lens, and use a spherometer's R to find the refractive index of the liquid.
theory:
A convex lens placed on a plane mirror with a needle above it forms an **inverted image that coincides with the needle** when the needle is at the **focus** of the lens: the rays leave the lens parallel, reflect normally from the mirror and retrace their path. Finding the point of **no parallax** gives the focal length **f₁**.

A few drops of liquid between the lens and the mirror form a **plano-concave liquid lens** in contact with the convex lens. The combination has a larger focal length **F**. For lenses in contact, **1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f_l**, so the liquid lens has **|f_l| = f₁F/(F − f₁)**.

For the liquid lens (one face of radius R, the other plane), **1/|f_l| = (n − 1)/R**, so **n = 1 + R/|f_l|**. The radius of curvature is found with a **spherometer**: **R = l²/(6h) + h/2**.

procedure.title: Set up
procedure.description: Place the convex lens on the plane mirror and clamp a needle above it, with its tip over the centre of the lens.

procedure.title: Remove parallax
procedure.description: Look down at the needle tip and its inverted image while moving your eye sideways. Raise or lower the needle until the image tip stays on the needle tip (no parallax).

procedure.title: Measure f₁
procedure.description: Measure the distance from the needle tip to the top of the lens (x₁) and to the mirror (x₂). Their mean is f₁. Repeat.

procedure.title: Add the liquid
procedure.description: Put a few drops of the liquid on the mirror and place the lens over it. Find the new no-parallax position and measure F in the same way. Repeat.

procedure.title: Find R
procedure.description: Use the spherometer readings (l and h) to find the radius of curvature R = l²/(6h) + h/2 of the lens surface.

procedure.title: Calculate n
procedure.description: Calculate |f_l| = f₁F/(F − f₁) and n = 1 + R/|f_l|.

observation: Without liquid the no-parallax distance gives f₁; with liquid it gives a larger F. The liquid lens focal length is |f_l| = f₁F/(F − f₁), and with R from the spherometer, n = 1 + R/|f_l| (about 1.33 for water, 1.44–1.48 for oils).

quiz.question: When the needle is at the focus of a convex lens resting on a plane mirror, its image:

options.text: Coincides with the needle, with no parallax

quiz.explanation: Rays from the focus leave the lens parallel, reflect normally from the mirror and retrace their path, so the inverted image forms at the needle itself.

quiz.question: Liquid placed between the convex lens and the plane mirror forms:
quiz.explanation: The liquid fills the space between the curved lower face of the lens and the flat mirror, so it takes the shape of a plano-concave lens.

quiz.question: With liquid under the lens, the no-parallax distance F compared with f₁ is:
quiz.explanation: The plano-concave liquid lens is diverging, so the combination has a longer focal length than the convex lens alone.

quiz.question: The focal length of the liquid lens (magnitude) is given by:
quiz.explanation: From 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f_l with f_l negative, |f_l| = f₁F/(F − f₁).

quiz.question: If the liquid lens has |f_l| = 60 cm and R = 20 cm, the refractive index of the liquid is:
The radius of curvature R of the lens surface is found with a:
quiz.explanation: A spherometer measures the height h of a spherical surface over its legs; R = l²/(6h) + h/2.

quiz.question: While removing parallax, the image moves with your eye. This means:

options.text: The needle is exactly at the focus
The image is nearer to your eye than the needle
The image is farther from your eye than the needle, so the needle should be lowered

quiz.explanation: Of two objects, the one farther from the eye moves with the eye. Here the image lies below the needle tip, so lower the needle.

quiz.question: Why is the focal length taken as the mean of x₁ (needle to lens top) and x₂ (needle to mirror)?

options.text: To give the distance to the middle of the lens
To remove the effect of the liquid
To measure the radius of curvature

quiz.explanation: The focal length is measured from the optical centre of the lens, which is midway between its top surface and the mirror.

title: Convex Lens (3D): Focal Length by the Displacement Method
summary: Fix an object and a screen more than 4f apart, slide a convex lens between them to find its two sharp positions, and find f = (D² − d²)/4D without measuring from the lens.
theory:
When an object and a screen are fixed a distance **D** apart and **D > 4f**, a convex lens between them gives a **sharp image at two positions**. At the first the image is **magnified**, at the second **diminished**: the object and image distances simply **interchange**.

If the two positions are a distance **d** apart, then **u = (D − d)/2** and **v = (D + d)/2**. The lens formula gives **f = uv/(u + v) = (D² − d²)/4D**.

The magnifications satisfy **m₁m₂ = 1**. Since only **D** and **d** are measured, the position of the optical centre of the lens does not matter. At **D = 4f** the two positions merge into one, and for D < 4f there is no sharp image at all.

procedure.title: Rough focal length
procedure.description: Estimate f roughly, then place the screen at a distance D greater than 4f from the object.

procedure.title: First sharp position
procedure.description: Slide the lens from near the object towards the screen until a sharp, magnified image appears. Record the lens position.

procedure.title: Second sharp position
procedure.description: Without moving the object or the screen, slide the lens further until a sharp, diminished image appears. Record this position.

procedure.title: Calculate f
procedure.description: Find d, the distance between the two lens positions, and f = (D² − d²)/4D.

procedure.title: Repeat
procedure.description: Repeat for at least three values of D and take the mean of f.

observation: For each D the two lens positions add up to about D (they are symmetric), the images are magnified and diminished, and f = (D² − d²)/4D comes out the same for every D.

quiz.question: In the displacement method, the focal length is given by:
quiz.explanation: With u = (D − d)/2 and v = (D + d)/2 in the lens formula, f = uv/(u + v) = (D² − d²)/4D.

quiz.question: Two sharp positions of the lens exist only when the object–screen distance D is:
quiz.explanation: The quadratic for the lens position has two real roots only if D² − 4Df > 0, that is D > 4f.

quiz.question: At the two lens positions, the object and image distances:
quiz.explanation: If the first position has u = x and v = D − x, the second has u = D − x and v = x.

quiz.question: The product of the magnifications at the two positions is:
quiz.explanation: m₁ = (D − x)/x and m₂ = x/(D − x), so m₁m₂ = 1, which also gives h = √(h₁h₂).

quiz.question: With D = 100 cm and d = 60 cm, the focal length is:
An advantage of the displacement method is that:

options.text: It works when D is less than f
The position of the optical centre of the lens need not be known

quiz.explanation: Only D and the distance d between the two lens positions are measured, so the uncertain position of the lens centre does not matter.

quiz.question: At the lens position nearer the object, the image on the screen is:
quiz.explanation: There u is small and v large, so the image is magnified; at the other position it is diminished.

quiz.question: When D is exactly 4f, the two sharp positions:

options.text: Move to the ends of the bench
Merge into one, at the midpoint

quiz.explanation: At D = 4f the two roots coincide at u = v = 2f, so there is only one sharp position, midway between object and screen.

title: Concave Lens (3D): Focal Length using a Convex Lens in Contact
summary: Measure a convex lens by the u–v method, put a concave lens in contact with it and measure the combination, then find the concave lens focal length from 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂.
theory:
A **concave lens** always forms a **virtual image**, so its focal length cannot be measured directly with a screen. Placed **in contact** with a stronger **convex lens**, the combination is converging and forms real images.

For thin lenses in contact the **powers add**: **1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂**. Measure f₁ (convex lens alone) and F (combination) by the **u–v method** (f = uv/(u + v)). Then **f₂ = f₁F/(f₁ − F)**, which is **negative** for the diverging lens.

Because the concave lens weakens the combination, **F > f₁**. f₂ depends on the small difference F − f₁, so careful readings are needed.

procedure.title: Convex lens alone
procedure.description: Mount the convex lens. For several object distances u, move the screen to the sharpest image and record v. Find f₁ = uv/(u + v) and its mean.

procedure.title: Put the lenses in contact
procedure.description: Place the concave lens in contact with the convex lens (press “Convex + concave in contact”).

procedure.title: Measure the combination
procedure.description: Repeat the u–v readings for the combination and find the mean F. Use larger u, since F is longer.

procedure.title: Calculate f₂
procedure.description: Calculate f₂ = f₁F/(f₁ − F). It is negative, showing a diverging lens. Its power is 100/f₂ dioptre (f in cm).

observation: The convex lens alone gives f₁; the combination gives a larger F. The focal length of the concave lens, f₂ = f₁F/(f₁ − F), is negative, typically −25 to −60 cm here.

quiz.question: Why can't the focal length of a concave lens be found directly with a screen?

options.text: It always forms a virtual image
It forms images only at infinity

quiz.explanation: A concave lens diverges light, so its images are virtual and cannot be caught on a screen.

quiz.question: For two thin lenses in contact, the focal length F of the combination is given by:
quiz.explanation: The powers of thin lenses in contact add: P = P₁ + P₂, so 1/F = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂.

quiz.question: For the combination to form a real image, the convex lens must:

options.text: Have a shorter focal length (greater power) than the concave lens
Have a longer focal length than the concave lens
Be thinner than the concave lens
Be placed far from the concave lens

quiz.explanation: The combined power P₁ + P₂ must be positive, so the convex lens must be the stronger of the two (|f₁| < |f₂|).

quiz.question: If f₁ = 12 cm and F = 20 cm, the focal length of the concave lens is:
Compared with the convex lens alone, the combination has:
quiz.explanation: Adding a diverging lens reduces the total power, so F > f₁.

quiz.question: The power of a concave lens of focal length −25 cm is:
quiz.explanation: P = 100/f (f in cm) = 100/(−25) = −4 dioptre.

quiz.question: Why do small errors in f₁ and F give a larger error in f₂?

options.text: Because f₂ depends on the difference F − f₁, which is small
Because the concave lens is virtual

quiz.explanation: f₂ = f₁F/(f₁ − F); the denominator is a small difference of two measured values, so its percentage error is large.

quiz.question: In the u–v method, f for each setting is found from:
quiz.explanation: From the lens formula with magnitudes, 1/u + 1/v = 1/f, so f = uv/(u + v).

title: Transistor (n-p-n, CE): Input and Output Characteristics
summary: Plot the input (I_B–V_BE) and output (I_C–V_CE) characteristics of an n-p-n transistor in common-emitter mode, and find its input resistance, output resistance and current gain β.
theory:
In the **common-emitter (CE)** configuration the input is applied between **base and emitter** and the output is taken between **collector and emitter**. For active operation the **base–emitter junction is forward biased** and the **collector–base junction is reverse biased**.

The **input characteristic** (I_B against V_BE at constant V_CE) is like that of a forward-biased diode. The **input resistance** is **r_i = ΔV_BE/ΔI_B**, about 1 kΩ.

The **output characteristic** (I_C against V_CE at constant I_B) rises steeply at small V_CE (**saturation region**), then becomes nearly flat (**active region**), where I_C is controlled by I_B. The **output resistance** is **r_o = ΔV_CE/ΔI_C**, tens of kΩ.

The **current gain** is **β = ΔI_C/ΔI_B** at constant V_CE, found from two or more output curves.

procedure.title: Input characteristic
procedure.description: Set V_CE to a fixed value (1 V) with the collector rheostat. Increase V_BB with the base rheostat in small steps, recording V_BE and I_B each time.

procedure.title: Second input curve (optional)
procedure.description: Repeat with V_CE = 5 V and compare the two input curves.

procedure.title: Output characteristic
procedure.description: Set I_B = 20 µA with the base rheostat. Vary V_CE from 0 to 10 V, recording I_C. After each change, readjust the base rheostat so I_B stays at 20 µA.

procedure.title: More output curves
procedure.description: Repeat for I_B = 40 µA and 60 µA.

procedure.title: Calculate
procedure.description: Find r_i from the steep part of the input curve, r_o from the slope of an output curve in the active region, and β = ΔI_C/ΔI_B at V_CE = 5 V.

observation: The input curve shows almost no I_B until V_BE ≈ 0.6 V, then a steep rise (r_i ≈ 1 kΩ). The output curves rise steeply up to V_CE ≈ 0.5 V and then are nearly flat (r_o of tens of kΩ). Equal steps of I_B give nearly equal steps of I_C, and β = ΔI_C/ΔI_B is typically 100–200.

quiz.question: In the common-emitter configuration, the input is applied between:
