quiz.explanation: In CE mode the input is between base and emitter and the output between collector and emitter; the emitter is common.

quiz.question: For normal (active) operation of an n-p-n transistor:

options.text: The base–emitter junction is forward biased and the collector–base junction reverse biased
The base–emitter junction is reverse biased

quiz.explanation: Forward bias at the emitter junction injects carriers; reverse bias at the collector junction collects them.

quiz.question: The input characteristic of a CE transistor resembles that of a:
quiz.explanation: I_B against V_BE is the characteristic of the forward-biased base–emitter junction, with a knee near 0.6–0.7 V for silicon.

quiz.question: The current gain β in CE mode is defined as:
quiz.explanation: β = ΔI_C/ΔI_B with V_CE held constant.

quiz.question: If I_B changes from 20 µA to 40 µA and I_C changes from 3.0 mA to 6.2 mA at the same V_CE, β is:
quiz.explanation: β = ΔI_C/ΔI_B = 3.2 mA / 20 µA = 160.

quiz.question: In the active region of the output characteristic, I_C:

options.text: Is almost independent of V_CE and controlled by I_B

quiz.explanation: Beyond about 1 V the output curves are nearly flat: I_C depends mainly on I_B, so the output resistance is high.

quiz.question: Typical values: the input resistance of a CE transistor is about ___ and its output resistance about ___.
quiz.explanation: r_i = ΔV_BE/ΔI_B is of the order of 1 kΩ; r_o = ΔV_CE/ΔI_C is tens of kilo-ohms.

quiz.question: While plotting an output characteristic, I_B drifts when V_CE is changed. You should:

options.text: Readjust the base rheostat to bring I_B back to its set value

quiz.explanation: Each output curve must be at constant I_B, so the base current is readjusted after every change of V_CE.

title: Logic Gates: Verifying Truth Tables with ICs
summary: Wire AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR gate ICs on a trainer board, verify each truth table with switches and an LED, and identify an unlabelled mystery IC.
theory:
A **logic gate** has inputs and an output that can each be **0 (0 V)** or **1 (+5 V)**. Its behaviour is described by a **truth table** listing the output for every combination of inputs.

**AND** (7408): **Y = A · B**. **OR** (7432): **Y = A + B**. **NOT** (7404): **Y = Ā**. **NAND** (7400): **Y = (A · B)‾**. **NOR** (7402): **Y = (A + B)‾**. **XOR** (7486): **Y = A ⊕ B**, 1 when the inputs differ.

**NAND and NOR are universal gates**: any other gate can be built from them. In 14-pin TTL ICs, **pin 14 is +5 V** and **pin 7 is ground**. Each IC holds four 2-input gates, or six NOT gates.

procedure.title: Connect the IC
procedure.description: Place the IC on the trainer with the notch towards pin 1. Connect pin 14 to +5 V and pin 7 to ground.

procedure.title: Wire inputs and output
procedure.description: Connect the gate's input pins to switches A and B and its output pin to the LED (check the pin diagram; on the 7402 the output is pin 1).

procedure.title: Fill the truth table
procedure.description: Set every combination of A and B. For each, note whether the LED is on (Y = 1) or off (Y = 0).

procedure.title: Identify the expression
procedure.description: Compare the completed table with the Boolean expressions and choose the one it matches.

procedure.title: Mystery IC
procedure.description: Find the truth table of an unlabelled IC and identify the gate inside it.

quiz.question: The output of an AND gate is 1 only when:
quiz.explanation: Y = A · B is 1 only for A = 1 and B = 1.

quiz.question: Which gate gives an output of 1 only when both inputs are 0?
quiz.explanation: NOR = NOT(A + B): A + B is 0 only when both inputs are 0, so the output is then 1.

quiz.question: The Boolean expression of a NAND gate is:
quiz.explanation: NAND is AND followed by NOT: Y = (A · B)‾.

quiz.question: Which gates are called universal gates?
quiz.explanation: Any logic gate can be built using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

quiz.question: An XOR gate gives Y = 1 when:
quiz.explanation: Y = A ⊕ B is 1 for A = 0, B = 1 and for A = 1, B = 0.

quiz.question: In a 7400-series IC, the supply is connected to:
quiz.explanation: For 14-pin TTL ICs, pin 14 is Vcc (+5 V) and pin 7 is ground.

quiz.question: How many rows does the truth table of a two-input gate have?
quiz.explanation: Each of the two inputs can be 0 or 1, giving 2² = 4 combinations.

quiz.question: The IC 7404 contains:
quiz.explanation: The 7404 is a hex inverter: six NOT gates in one package.

title: Galvanometer: Conversion into a Voltmeter and an Ammeter
summary: Use the galvanometer's resistance and figure of merit to calculate a series resistance (voltmeter) or a shunt wire (ammeter), set it, and verify the converted meter against a standard meter.
theory:
A galvanometer with **N** divisions and figure of merit **k** gives full-scale deflection for **I_g = N k**, typically below 1 mA.

**Voltmeter:** connect a **high resistance R in series**. At the full range V₀ the current must be I_g: **I_g(G + R) = V₀**, so **R = V₀/I_g − G**.

**Ammeter:** connect a **low resistance S (shunt) in parallel**. At the full range I₀ only I_g flows through the galvanometer: **I_g G = (I₀ − I_g)S**, so **S = I_g G/(I₀ − I_g)**. A shunt wire of resistance ρ per cm needs a length **l = S/ρ**.

The converted meter's scale reads **(θ/N) × full range**, and it is checked against a standard meter.

procedure.title: Calculate I_g
procedure.description: From G and k (half-deflection experiment), find I_g = N k.

procedure.title: Voltmeter
procedure.description: Calculate R = V₀/I_g − G, set it in the resistance box in series with the galvanometer, and connect the combination in parallel with a standard voltmeter across a potential divider.

procedure.title: Verify the voltmeter
procedure.description: For several settings of the rheostat, compare the standard voltmeter with the converted reading (θ/N) × V₀.

procedure.title: Ammeter
procedure.description: Calculate S = I_g G/(I₀ − I_g) and the wire length l = S/ρ. Connect the shunt wire across the galvanometer and the combination in series with a standard ammeter.

procedure.title: Verify the ammeter
procedure.description: For several currents, compare the standard ammeter with the converted reading (θ/N) × I₀.

observation: With the calculated R (or shunt length) the converted meter agrees with the standard meter over the whole range, and a graph of converted against standard readings lies on the 45° line.

quiz.question: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, we connect:
quiz.explanation: A high series resistance limits the current to I_g when the full voltage V₀ is applied.

quiz.question: To convert a galvanometer into an ammeter, we connect:
quiz.explanation: The shunt carries most of the current, so only I_g flows through the galvanometer at full scale.

quiz.question: The series resistance for a voltmeter of range V₀ is:
quiz.explanation: I_g(G + R) = V₀ gives R = V₀/I_g − G.

quiz.question: The shunt for an ammeter of range I₀ is:
quiz.explanation: The galvanometer and shunt have the same p.d.: I_g G = (I₀ − I_g)S.

quiz.question: A galvanometer of G = 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 1 mA. The resistance needed to make a 0–5 V voltmeter is:
Compared with the galvanometer, the resistance of an ammeter made from it is:
quiz.explanation: The shunt in parallel makes the total resistance smaller than S itself, which is very small. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance.

quiz.question: The full-scale current of a galvanometer with figure of merit k and N divisions is:
quiz.explanation: Each division needs a current k, so N divisions need I_g = N k.

quiz.question: If a converted voltmeter reads higher than the standard voltmeter, the series resistance is:

options.text: Too small, so it should be increased
Too large, so it should be decreased

quiz.explanation: Too small a series resistance lets too much current through the galvanometer, so it over-reads.

title: Tangent Galvanometer (3D): Reduction Factor and B_H
summary: Set the coil in the magnetic meridian, pass currents through 2, 5 or 50 turns, read both pointer ends for direct and reversed current, and find the reduction factor K and the Earth's horizontal field B_H.
theory:
A current **I** in a circular coil of **n** turns and radius **r** produces a field **B = μ₀nI/2r** at its centre, along the axis of the coil.

If the plane of the coil is in the **magnetic meridian**, this field is perpendicular to the Earth's horizontal field **B_H**. A compass needle at the centre sets along the resultant, at an angle **θ** to the meridian, where **tan θ = B/B_H** (tangent law).

So **I = K tan θ**, where the **reduction factor** is **K = 2rB_H/(μ₀n)**. From the readings, **K = I/tan θ** and **B_H = μ₀nK/2r**. The radius is found from the circumference: **r = C/2π**.

The instrument is most sensitive near **θ = 45°**, so currents are chosen to give deflections between 30° and 60°. Reading both ends of the pointer removes the error from an off-centre pivot, and reversing the current removes the error from imperfect setting in the meridian.

procedure.title: Set in the meridian
procedure.description: Level the instrument. With no current, turn the whole instrument until the coil is in the magnetic meridian and the aluminium pointer reads 0–0.

procedure.title: Connect the circuit
procedure.description: Connect the battery, key, rheostat, ammeter and commutator in series with the chosen number of turns (2, 5 or 50).

procedure.title: Direct current
procedure.description: Close the key, adjust the rheostat for a deflection between 30° and 60°, and read both ends of the pointer (θ₁, θ₂) and the ammeter.

procedure.title: Reverse the current
procedure.description: Reverse the current with the commutator, keeping the same current, and read both ends again (θ₃, θ₄).

procedure.title: Repeat
procedure.description: Repeat for 3–4 different currents. For each, find mean θ and K = I/tan θ.

procedure.title: Calculate B_H
procedure.description: Measure the circumference C of the coil with a thread, find r = C/2π, and calculate B_H = μ₀nK/2r using the mean K.

observation: I/tan θ is constant for a given number of turns (the tangent law). The reduction factor K is smaller for more turns, while B_H comes out about 3–4 × 10⁻⁵ T for every set of turns.

quiz.question: The tangent galvanometer is based on the relation:
quiz.explanation: The needle sets along the resultant of two perpendicular fields, so tan θ = B/B_H.

quiz.question: Before passing current, the plane of the coil is set:
quiz.explanation: Only then is the coil's field (along its axis) perpendicular to B_H.

quiz.question: The reduction factor K of a tangent galvanometer is:
quiz.explanation: From μ₀nI/2r = B_H tan θ, I = (2rB_H/μ₀n) tan θ.

quiz.question: Why are deflections kept between 30° and 60°?

options.text: The scale is only marked to 60°
The instrument is most sensitive near 45°

quiz.explanation: The fractional error in tan θ, dθ/(sin θ cos θ), is least at θ = 45°.

quiz.question: Reading both ends of the pointer removes the error due to:
quiz.explanation: If the pivot is off-centre, one end reads high and the other low; their mean is correct.

quiz.question: Reversing the current with the commutator removes the error due to:

options.text: The coil not being exactly in the magnetic meridian

quiz.explanation: If the coil is slightly off the meridian, deflections on the two sides differ; their mean cancels the error.

quiz.question: If the number of turns is increased from 5 to 50 (other things the same), the reduction factor:
quiz.explanation: K = 2rB_H/μ₀n is inversely proportional to n.

quiz.question: A tangent galvanometer cannot be used near the magnetic poles because there:

options.text: The coil cannot be set in the meridian

quiz.explanation: At the poles the Earth's field is almost vertical, so B_H ≈ 0 and the needle has no horizontal restoring field.

title: Acid–Base Titration: Strength of NaOH, KOH or HCl
summary: Rinse and fill a burette, pipette standard oxalic acid, titrate to the first permanent pale pink with phenolphthalein, read the burette yourself, get concordant titres, and calculate molarity and strength. Includes double titration with NaOH as a link solution to estimate HCl.
theory:
In an acid–base titration a solution of known concentration (the **standard solution**) reacts with a solution of unknown concentration. The **end point** is shown by an indicator: **phenolphthalein** is colourless in acid and turns **pale pink** as soon as there is a slight excess of alkali.

**Oxalic acid with alkali:** H₂C₂O₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂C₂O₄ + 2H₂O. So n₁ = 1 (acid) and n₂ = 2 (base).

**Molarity equation:** **M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂**. With V₁ = 20 mL of standard oxalic acid and V₂ the concordant burette reading, M₂ = 2M₁V₁/V₂.

**Strength (g/L) = molarity × molar mass** (NaOH 40, KOH 56, HCl 36.5).

**Link solution (double titration):** to estimate HCl, NaOH of unknown strength is first standardised against oxalic acid (titration I). The same NaOH is then titrated against the HCl (titration II): HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, so M(HCl) × 20 = M(NaOH) × V(NaOH).

Titres are repeated until two agree within 0.1 mL (**concordant values**).

procedure.title: Rinse
procedure.description: Rinse the burette with the alkali it will hold and the pipette with the acid it will measure. Rinse the conical flask with distilled water only.

procedure.title: Fill the burette
procedure.description: Fill the burette with the alkali, remove the funnel, and run out a little to remove the air bubble from the nozzle.

procedure.title: Pipette the acid
procedure.description: Pipette 20 mL of the standard oxalic acid (or HCl) into the conical flask on a white tile, and add two drops of phenolphthalein.

procedure.title: Initial reading
procedure.description: Read the bottom of the meniscus with your eye at its level and note the initial reading.

procedure.title: Titrate
procedure.description: Run in the alkali while swirling. Do a rough titration first; then add drop by drop near the end point until the first permanent pale pink.

procedure.title: Final reading
procedure.description: Note the final reading. The titre is final − initial. Repeat until two titres agree within 0.1 mL.

procedure.title: Calculate
procedure.description: Use M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂ with the concordant titre to find the molarity, then strength = molarity × molar mass.

observation: The colourless acid turns pale pink at the end point. Repeated accurate titres agree within 0.1 mL; the concordant value gives the molarity and strength of the unknown solution.

quiz.question: The colour change of phenolphthalein at the end point (alkali added to acid) is:
quiz.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and turns pink as soon as there is a slight excess of alkali.

quiz.question: The burette should be rinsed with:

options.text: The solution it is to hold

quiz.explanation: Water left inside would dilute the solution and make the titre too high.

quiz.question: The conical flask should be rinsed with:
quiz.explanation: Water does not change the amount of acid pipetted in, but acid left on the walls would add extra acid.

quiz.question: For oxalic acid and NaOH, the values of n₁ (acid) and n₂ (base) in M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂ are:
quiz.explanation: H₂C₂O₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂C₂O₄ + 2H₂O: one mole of acid reacts with two moles of base.

quiz.question: 20 mL of 0.05 M oxalic acid needs 20 mL of NaOH. The molarity of NaOH is:
If an air bubble in the burette nozzle is not removed before the initial reading, the titre will be:
quiz.explanation: The bubble fills with liquid during the titration, so the burette shows more volume than actually entered the flask.

quiz.question: Strength of 0.1 M NaOH in g/L is:
quiz.explanation: Strength = molarity × molar mass = 0.1 × 40 = 4.0 g/L.

quiz.question: Why is NaOH called a link solution when HCl is estimated using standard oxalic acid?

options.text: Its strength is found first using oxalic acid, and then used to find the HCl

quiz.explanation: NaOH links the two titrations: titration I standardises it, titration II uses it to find the HCl.

title: Salt Analysis: Identify the Anion and Cation
summary: Analyse an unknown simple salt systematically: preliminary tests, anion tests and cation group tests, writing the observation and inference for each, and report the salt only after confirmatory tests. A new random salt each time.
theory:
A simple salt contains one **anion** (acid radical) and one **cation** (basic radical). They are identified by characteristic reactions: gases, precipitates, colours and smells.

**Anions** are first detected with dilute and concentrated H₂SO₄ (carbonate: effervescence of CO₂; acetate: smell of vinegar; chloride: HCl gas giving white fumes with NH₃; nitrate: brown NO₂ fumes with copper) and then confirmed: lime water, AgNO₃, brown ring test, BaCl₂, neutral FeCl₃ or the ester test.

**Cations:** NH₄⁺ is tested first with NaOH (ammonia). The others are separated into **groups** by group reagents, which must be used in order: group I dil. HCl (Pb²⁺), group III NH₄Cl + NH₄OH (Al³⁺), group IV H₂S in ammoniacal solution (Zn²⁺), group V (NH₄)₂CO₃ (Ba²⁺, Ca²⁺), group VI Na₂HPO₄ (Mg²⁺). The group precipitate is then confirmed by a specific test.

Each test is recorded as **experiment – observation – inference**, and an ion is reported only after its confirmatory test.

procedure.title: Preliminary tests
procedure.description: Note the colour and appearance, and dissolve a little salt in distilled water to make the original solution (OS).

procedure.title: Test for NH₄⁺
procedure.description: Warm the salt with NaOH solution. A smell of ammonia that turns red litmus blue shows NH₄⁺.

procedure.title: Anion: preliminary
procedure.description: Treat the salt with dil. H₂SO₄, then with conc. H₂SO₄ (and copper turnings), and note gases, fumes and smells.

procedure.title: Anion: confirmatory
procedure.description: Do the confirmatory test suggested by the preliminary tests (lime water, AgNO₃, brown ring, BaCl₂, FeCl₃ or ester test).

procedure.title: Cation: group tests
procedure.description: Add the group reagents to the OS in order (I, III, IV, V, VI) until a precipitate appears.

procedure.title: Cation: confirmatory
procedure.description: Confirm the cation of that group with its specific test (KI, blue lake, potassium ferrocyanide, flame test, ammonium oxalate, phosphate).

procedure.title: Report
procedure.description: Write the anion and cation, and the name of the salt.

observation: Each test gives a characteristic observation; the preliminary tests narrow down the possibilities and the confirmatory tests establish one anion and one cation.

quiz.question: A salt gives brisk effervescence with dil. H₂SO₄, and the gas turns lime water milky. The anion is:
quiz.explanation: CO₂ from a carbonate turns lime water milky (CaCO₃).

quiz.question: The brown ring test is used to confirm:
quiz.explanation: NO from the nitrate forms a brown complex with Fe²⁺ at the junction of the layers.

quiz.question: A white precipitate with AgNO₃ that dissolves in NH₄OH shows:
quiz.explanation: AgCl dissolves in ammonia forming [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.

quiz.question: The group reagent for group III cations is:
quiz.explanation: Group III hydroxides (e.g. Al(OH)₃) precipitate with NH₄OH in the presence of NH₄Cl.

quiz.question: An apple-green flame in the flame test indicates:
quiz.explanation: Barium gives an apple-green flame; calcium gives brick red.

quiz.question: Why is NH₄Cl added along with NH₄OH in group III?

options.text: To suppress the ionisation of NH₄OH so that only group III hydroxides precipitate

quiz.explanation: The common ion NH₄⁺ lowers the OH⁻ concentration, so Mg(OH)₂ and others of later groups do not precipitate.

quiz.question: Smell of vinegar with dil. H₂SO₄ and a deep red colour with neutral FeCl₃ indicate:
quiz.explanation: Acetic acid smells of vinegar; acetate gives a red complex with Fe³⁺.

quiz.question: Ammonium ion is tested by:

options.text: Warming with NaOH: ammonia turns red litmus blue

quiz.explanation: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O on warming; ammonia is alkaline and has a pungent smell.

title: Organic Analysis: Tests for Functional Groups
summary: Identify the functional group in an unknown organic compound (alcohol, phenol, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid or primary aromatic amine) with preliminary and confirmatory tests, writing the observation and inference for each.
theory:
Each functional group has characteristic reactions.

**Carboxylic acids** turn blue litmus red and liberate CO₂ from sodium bicarbonate (brisk effervescence). With ethanol and conc. H₂SO₄ they form fruity-smelling esters.

**Phenols** give a **violet** colour with neutral FeCl₃ and a white precipitate (2,4,6-tribromophenol) with bromine water.

**Aldehydes and ketones** (carbonyl compounds) give a yellow-orange precipitate with **2,4-DNP**. Aldehydes are reducing: they give a **silver mirror** with Tollens’ reagent and a pink colour with Schiff’s reagent; aliphatic aldehydes also give a brick-red precipitate with Fehling’s solution. Ketones do not; methyl ketones give a red colour in the **sodium nitroprusside** test.

**Alcohols** liberate hydrogen with sodium and turn yellow **ceric ammonium nitrate** red.

**Primary aromatic amines** (aniline) dissolve in dilute HCl, give an **orange-red azo dye** after diazotisation and coupling with β-naphthol, and an offensive smell in the **carbylamine test**.

The **iodoform test** (yellow precipitate) shows a CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)– group.

procedure.title: Physical examination
procedure.description: Note the state, colour and smell of the compound.

procedure.title: Test for acid
procedure.description: Test with blue litmus and sodium bicarbonate solution.

procedure.title: Test for phenol
procedure.description: Add neutral FeCl₃ solution; a violet colour shows a phenol. Bromine water gives a white precipitate.

procedure.title: Test for carbonyl
procedure.description: Add 2,4-DNP reagent. A yellow-orange precipitate shows an aldehyde or ketone; then use Tollens’ (aldehyde) or sodium nitroprusside (ketone).

procedure.title: Test for amine
procedure.description: Shake with dil. HCl; confirm with the azo dye test or the carbylamine test.

procedure.title: Test for alcohol
procedure.description: Add ceric ammonium nitrate; a red colour shows an alcohol.

procedure.title: Report
procedure.description: Write the functional group, confirmed by its confirmatory test.

observation: Only the tests for the functional group present are positive; its confirmatory test gives the characteristic colour, precipitate, mirror or smell.

quiz.question: A compound gives brisk effervescence with NaHCO₃. The functional group is:
quiz.explanation: Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than carbonic acid and liberate CO₂.

quiz.question: Neutral FeCl₃ gives a violet colour with:
quiz.explanation: Phenols form a coloured complex with Fe³⁺.

quiz.question: Both aldehydes and ketones give a yellow-orange precipitate with:
quiz.explanation: 2,4-DNP forms a 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone with any carbonyl group.

quiz.question: The silver mirror test (Tollens’ reagent) is given by:
quiz.explanation: Aldehydes reduce Ag⁺ to metallic silver; ketones do not.

quiz.question: Benzaldehyde does not give a positive test with:
quiz.explanation: Aromatic aldehydes do not reduce Fehling’s solution.

quiz.question: The carbylamine test is used to detect:
quiz.explanation: Primary amines with CHCl₃ and alcoholic KOH give isocyanides with an offensive smell.

quiz.question: Which of these gives the iodoform test?
quiz.explanation: Acetone has a CH₃CO– group, which gives yellow iodoform with I₂ and NaOH.

quiz.question: Aniline is converted into an orange-red dye by:

options.text: Diazotisation, then coupling with alkaline β-naphthol

quiz.explanation: The diazonium salt couples with β-naphthol to form an azo dye.

title: Quadrat Method: Population Density, Frequency and Abundance
summary: Place 1 m × 1 m quadrats at random in a field, count four plant species yourself in a close-up, and calculate density, frequency and abundance. Then compare your estimate with the whole field.
theory:
A **quadrat** is a square frame (here 1 m × 1 m) used to sample vegetation. Counting every plant in a field is impractical, so several quadrats are placed **at random** and the plants inside are counted.

**Density** = total number of individuals of a species ÷ total number of quadrats studied. It is the number per unit area (per m² here).

**Frequency (%)** = (number of quadrats in which the species occurs ÷ total number of quadrats studied) × 100. It shows how widely the species is spread.

**Abundance** = total number of individuals ÷ number of quadrats in which the species occurs. It shows how plentiful the species is where it grows.

A species growing in patches (clumped) has low frequency but high abundance; a species spread evenly has high frequency. Larger samples give estimates closer to the true values.

procedure.title: Place a quadrat
procedure.description: Place a 1 m × 1 m quadrat at random in the study area.

procedure.title: Count
procedure.description: Identify the species inside it and count the individuals of each. Count a plant only if it is rooted inside the frame.

procedure.title: Repeat
procedure.description: Repeat for at least 10 quadrats spread at random over the area, without overlapping.

procedure.title: Tabulate
procedure.description: Record the counts in a table: quadrat number against the number of each species.

procedure.title: Calculate
procedure.description: For each species find the total number, the number of quadrats in which it occurs, and calculate density, frequency and abundance.

observation: Common, evenly spread species have high density and high frequency; species in patches have low frequency but high abundance; rare species may be missed with few quadrats.

quiz.question: Population density is calculated as:
quiz.explanation: Density is the average number per quadrat (per unit area) over all quadrats studied.

quiz.question: A species is found in 6 of 10 quadrats. Its frequency is:
A species has 30 individuals in 5 of the 10 quadrats studied. Its abundance is:
quiz.explanation: Abundance = 30 ÷ 5 quadrats of occurrence = 6.

quiz.question: Why are quadrats placed at random?

options.text: So that the sample represents the whole area without bias

quiz.explanation: Choosing places by hand tends to favour interesting spots and biases the estimate.

quiz.question: A species with low frequency but high abundance most likely:
quiz.explanation: It is missing from many quadrats but plentiful where it occurs.

quiz.question: Increasing the number of quadrats studied generally:

options.text: Brings the estimate closer to the true value

quiz.explanation: A larger random sample represents the area better.

quiz.question: The size of the quadrat used in this experiment is:
quiz.explanation: A 1 m² quadrat is suitable for herbaceous vegetation; density is then per m².

quiz.question: If a species occurs in every quadrat studied, its frequency is:
quiz.explanation: It occurs in all quadrats, so frequency = 100%.

title: Salivary Amylase: Effect of Temperature and pH
summary: Add saliva to starch at six temperatures (or six pH values), test a drop from each tube with iodine every minute on a spot tile, mark the achromic point yourself, and find the optimum from the rate 1/t. Includes boiled saliva and an ice tube you can warm up.
theory:
**Salivary amylase** (ptyalin) is an enzyme in saliva that hydrolyses **starch** into **maltose**.

The progress of digestion is followed with **iodine**: starch gives a **blue-black** colour; as it is broken down into dextrins the colour changes through violet and reddish brown; when no starch is left, the drop keeps the **yellowish colour of iodine**. The first test that gives no blue colour is the **achromic point**.

The **rate** of enzyme action is taken as **1 / time to reach the achromic point**.

**Temperature:** activity rises with temperature up to the **optimum (about 37 °C)**. At low temperature the enzyme is **inactive but not destroyed** (activity returns on warming). At high temperature, and on boiling, the enzyme (a protein) is **denatured** and permanently loses its activity.

**pH:** salivary amylase works best near **pH 6.8**. Strongly acidic or alkaline conditions change the shape of the active site and stop its action, which is why salivary amylase stops working in the acidic stomach.

procedure.title: Prepare tubes
procedure.description: Take 2 mL of 1% starch solution in each of six test tubes. Keep them at different temperatures (ice, 20, 37, 45, 60 °C) or in buffers of different pH at 37 °C.

procedure.title: Boiled saliva
procedure.description: For the control, boil some diluted saliva and cool it.

procedure.title: Start
procedure.description: Add 1 mL of diluted saliva to each tube at the same moment and start the stopwatch.

procedure.title: Test every minute
procedure.description: Every minute, put one drop from each tube into a cavity of a spot tile containing a drop of iodine solution.

procedure.title: Achromic point
procedure.description: Note the time at which the drop no longer gives a blue colour with iodine.

procedure.title: Calculate
procedure.description: Calculate the rate as 1/time, plot rate against temperature (or pH), and find the optimum.

observation: The achromic point is reached fastest at about 37 °C and pH 6.8. At 0 °C, 60 °C, with boiled saliva, and at pH 4 or 9 the drops stay blue-black. The cold tube digests starch once warmed to 37 °C.

quiz.question: Salivary amylase converts starch into:
quiz.explanation: Amylase hydrolyses starch to the disaccharide maltose.

quiz.question: With iodine, starch gives a:
quiz.explanation: Starch forms a blue-black complex with iodine.

quiz.question: The achromic point is reached when:

options.text: The drop no longer gives a blue colour with iodine

quiz.explanation: No starch is left, so iodine keeps its own colour.

quiz.question: If the achromic point is reached in 5 minutes, the rate of enzyme action is:
quiz.explanation: Rate = 1/t = 1/5 = 0.2 per minute.

quiz.question: The optimum temperature of salivary amylase is about:
quiz.explanation: It works best at body temperature.

quiz.question: Boiled saliva does not digest starch because:

options.text: Iodine does not work after boiling

quiz.explanation: Heat permanently destroys the 3D structure of the enzyme protein.

quiz.question: A tube kept in ice shows no digestion, but digests starch when warmed to 37 °C. This shows that low temperature:
quiz.explanation: At low temperature molecules move slowly; the enzyme is not destroyed.

quiz.question: Salivary amylase stops working in the stomach because:

options.text: There is no starch in the stomach

quiz.explanation: The optimum pH of salivary amylase is about 6.8; the stomach is about pH 2.

title: Mitosis in Onion Root Tip: Stages and Mitotic Index
summary: Prepare an acetocarmine squash of an onion root tip step by step, examine cells under the microscope, identify interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, and calculate the mitotic index from several fields.
theory:
Root tips grow by **mitosis** in the **meristem** just behind the tip, so a squash of an onion root tip shows cells at every stage of division.

**Preparation:** root tips are **fixed** in Farmer’s fluid (acetic acid : alcohol = 1 : 3) to stop division and preserve the cells, **hydrolysed** in 1N HCl (dissolves the middle lamella so cells separate), **stained** with acetocarmine (stains chromosomes red), mounted and gently **squashed** into a single layer.

**Stages:**
- **Interphase:** round nucleus with nucleolus; chromosomes not visible.
- **Prophase:** chromosomes condense into visible threads.
- **Metaphase:** chromosomes line up at the equatorial plate.
- **Anaphase:** sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles (V-shaped).
- **Telophase:** two daughter nuclei form; a cell plate forms between them (cytokinesis in plant cells).

**Mitotic index** = (number of dividing cells ÷ total number of cells) × 100. Most cells are seen in interphase because it is the longest phase of the cell cycle; among the stages of mitosis, prophase is the longest and anaphase the shortest.

procedure.title: Grow roots
procedure.description: Grow onion roots by keeping the bulb on a beaker of water for a few days.

procedure.title: Cut and fix
procedure.description: Cut 1–2 cm root tips and fix them in Farmer’s fluid.

procedure.title: Hydrolyse
procedure.description: Warm the tips in 1N HCl at about 60 °C for a few minutes and wash.

procedure.title: Stain
procedure.description: Stain with acetocarmine for about 10 minutes.

procedure.title: Mount and squash
procedure.description: Place a tip on a slide in a drop of glycerine, cover with a coverslip and squash gently.

procedure.title: Observe
procedure.description: Observe under low and then high power; identify the stages of mitosis.

procedure.title: Count
procedure.description: Count interphase and dividing cells in several fields and calculate the mitotic index.

observation: Most cells are in interphase. Dividing cells show prophase (threads), metaphase (equatorial plate), anaphase (chromosomes moving to poles) and telophase (two nuclei, cell plate). Prophase cells are the commonest dividing cells and anaphase the rarest.

quiz.question: Onion root tips are used to study mitosis because:

options.text: The meristem near the tip divides actively
They are easy to stain blue

quiz.explanation: The root apical meristem divides continuously by mitosis.

quiz.question: Farmer’s fluid used for fixing contains:
quiz.explanation: It kills and preserves the cells at their stage of division.

quiz.question: The root tips are warmed in 1N HCl to:

options.text: Dissolve the middle lamella so that cells separate

quiz.explanation: Hydrolysis softens the tissue so that it spreads when squashed.

quiz.question: Chromosomes arranged at the equatorial plate are seen in:
quiz.explanation: At metaphase chromosomes align at the middle of the spindle.

quiz.question: V-shaped chromosomes moving towards opposite poles are seen in:
quiz.explanation: In anaphase the centromeres split and chromatids are pulled to the poles.

quiz.question: In a field, 90 cells are in interphase and 10 cells are dividing. The mitotic index is:
quiz.explanation: Mitotic index = 10 ÷ 100 × 100 = 10%.

quiz.question: Most cells in the squash are in interphase because:

options.text: Interphase is the longest phase of the cell cycle
Interphase cells take up more stain
Dividing cells are destroyed by HCl

quiz.explanation: Cells spend most of the cycle in interphase, so most are found there.

quiz.question: In plant cells, cytokinesis takes place by:
quiz.explanation: A cell plate forms in the middle and grows outwards to separate the daughter cells.

title: Mendelian Inheritance: Monohybrid and Dihybrid Ratios
summary: Simulate Mendel’s crosses by drawing gamete beads from two bags: identify each zygote’s seed type, fill a Punnett square with your counts, and see the 3 : 1 and 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratios emerge from chance.
theory:
Mendel crossed pea plants differing in contrasting characters, such as round (R) and wrinkled (r) seeds, or yellow (Y) and green (y) seeds. **R** and **Y** are **dominant**: one dominant allele is enough to show the character.

**Law of segregation:** the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so a heterozygote **Rr** produces **R** and **r** gametes in equal numbers. Random fertilisation of Rr × Rr gives genotypes **RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1** and phenotypes **round : wrinkled = 3 : 1**.

**Law of independent assortment:** in a dihybrid **RrYy** the genes for shape and colour segregate independently, giving four kinds of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal numbers. RrYy × RrYy gives **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**.

In this model two bags of beads represent the gametes of the two parents. Drawing one bead from each bag at random is fertilisation. Because the process is random, small samples differ from the expected ratio; large samples come close to it.

procedure.title: Prepare the bags
procedure.description: Put equal numbers of beads for R and r (or RY, Ry, rY, ry) into each of two bags: the gametes of the two heterozygous parents.

procedure.title: Draw
procedure.description: Without looking, draw one bead from each bag. The pair is the genotype of the zygote.

procedure.title: Record
procedure.description: Write the genotype and the phenotype it produces, and return the beads to their bags.

procedure.title: Repeat
procedure.description: Repeat many times (at least 50 for a monohybrid and 100 for a dihybrid cross).

procedure.title: Analyse
procedure.description: Count each phenotype and genotype and compare the observed ratio with the expected 3 : 1 or 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

observation: Round and wrinkled seeds appear in about 3 : 1, genotypes RR : Rr : rr in about 1 : 2 : 1, and the dihybrid classes in about 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, closer to the expected ratio as the number of draws increases.

quiz.question: A cross between two heterozygous round-seeded plants (Rr × Rr) gives a phenotypic ratio of:
quiz.explanation: RR and Rr are round, rr is wrinkled: 3 round : 1 wrinkled.

quiz.question: The genotypic ratio of the monohybrid F₂ generation is:
quiz.explanation: RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1.

quiz.question: Why is a seed with genotype Rr round?
quiz.explanation: One dominant allele is enough to show the dominant character.

quiz.question: The dihybrid F₂ phenotypic ratio is:
quiz.explanation: Two independently assorting genes, each 3 : 1, give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

quiz.question: How many kinds of gametes does RrYy produce?
quiz.explanation: RY, Ry, rY and ry in equal numbers.

quiz.question: Drawing one bead from each bag in this experiment represents:
quiz.explanation: Each bead is a gamete; a pair drawn together forms a zygote.

quiz.question: Why are the beads returned to the bags after each draw?

options.text: To keep the proportions of the two kinds of gametes equal

quiz.explanation: Without replacement the proportions change and the probabilities are no longer 1/2.

title: Pollen Germination on a Slide: Effect of Sucrose
summary: Sow pollen in 0–20% sucrose (with or without boric acid), look under the microscope after 10, 20 and 30 minutes, mark the germinated grains yourself, and find the concentration that gives the highest percentage germination.
theory:
On the stigma, a compatible pollen grain absorbs water and sugars and **germinates**: the vegetative cell grows out through a germ pore as a **pollen tube**, which carries the male gametes to the ovule.

The same can be seen on a slide in a **sucrose solution**. Sucrose provides food for the growing tube and keeps the medium close to the grain’s own concentration. In **plain water** many grains **burst** because water enters them by osmosis; in a **strong** sugar solution water is drawn out and few grains germinate. A moderate concentration (about **10%** for many species) gives the highest germination. **Boric acid** (boron) improves germination and tube growth.

A grain is counted as **germinated** when its pollen tube is at least as long as the diameter of the grain.

**% germination = (number of germinated grains ÷ total number of grains in the field) × 100.**

procedure.title: Prepare media
procedure.description: Prepare sucrose solutions of 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20% (with a trace of boric acid if required).

procedure.title: Sow pollen
procedure.description: Put a drop of medium on a clean cavity slide and dust pollen from a freshly opened flower onto it; cover with a coverslip.

procedure.title: Incubate
procedure.description: Keep the slide in a moist chamber at room temperature.

procedure.title: Observe
procedure.description: Observe under the microscope after 10, 20 and 30 minutes.

procedure.title: Count
procedure.description: In each field count the total grains and the germinated grains (tube at least as long as the grain is wide).

procedure.title: Calculate
procedure.description: Calculate % germination and plot it against sucrose concentration.

observation: Pollen tubes appear and grow longer with time. Germination is highest at a moderate sucrose concentration (about 10%), low in water (where many grains burst) and in strong sucrose. Boric acid increases germination.

quiz.question: A pollen grain is counted as germinated when:

options.text: Its pollen tube is at least as long as the grain’s diameter

quiz.explanation: This simple rule is applied the same way to every grain.

quiz.question: In plain water many pollen grains burst because:
quiz.explanation: Water is hypotonic to the grain, so water moves in until the grain bursts.

quiz.question: Few grains germinate in 20% sucrose because:

options.text: Water is drawn out of the grains

quiz.explanation: A strong solution is hypertonic and the grain loses water.

quiz.question: Boric acid is added to the medium because boron:
quiz.explanation: Boron is needed for normal pollen tube growth.

quiz.question: In a field of 40 grains, 26 have germinated. The % germination is:
The pollen tube develops from the:
quiz.explanation: The vegetative cell grows out as the pollen tube; the generative cell gives the male gametes.

quiz.question: The pollen tube emerges through the:
quiz.explanation: Germ pores are thin regions of the exine where sporopollenin is absent.

quiz.question: Why is the slide kept in a moist chamber?

options.text: To stop the medium from drying

quiz.explanation: If the drop dries, the grains cannot germinate.

title: Soil Analysis: Texture, Moisture, pH and Water Holding Capacity
summary: Test soils from a river bank, a kitchen garden and a paddy field: read sedimentation layers for texture, weigh before and after oven drying for moisture, match pH paper, and measure water holding capacity. Then relate the soils to the plants that grow there.
theory:
Soil properties decide which plants can grow in a place.

**Texture** depends on the proportions of sand (coarse), silt (medium) and clay (very fine) particles. When soil is shaken with water and allowed to settle, sand settles first, then silt, then clay; the thickness of each layer gives its percentage. **Sandy** soils are mostly sand, **clayey** soils have much clay, and **loamy** soils are a balanced mixture, best for most crops.

**Moisture content (%) = (W₁ − W₂) ÷ W₁ × 100**, where W₁ is the fresh mass and W₂ the mass after drying at 105 °C.

**pH** is found with universal indicator paper on a soil–water filtrate. Many Kerala soils are acidic.

**Water holding capacity** is the amount of water a soil can retain against gravity: **water held ÷ mass of dry soil × 100**. Fine clay particles leave small pores that hold water by capillarity, so clayey soils hold much more water than sandy soils, through which water drains quickly.

Sandy soils support plants adapted to dryness; clayey, waterlogged soils suit plants such as rice; loamy soils suit most crops.

procedure.title: Collect samples
procedure.description: Collect soil from different sites from about 10 cm depth and note the plants growing there.

procedure.title: Texture
procedure.description: Shake soil with water in a measuring cylinder, let it settle for a day, and measure the sand, silt and clay layers.

procedure.title: Moisture
procedure.description: Weigh 50 g of fresh soil, dry it in an oven at 105 °C, cool and weigh again; calculate the moisture %.

procedure.title: pH
procedure.description: Shake soil with distilled water, filter, and test the filtrate with universal pH paper.

procedure.title: Water holding capacity
procedure.description: Place 50 g of dry soil on a filter paper in a funnel, pour 100 mL of water, collect the water that drains, and calculate the water held.

procedure.title: Correlate
procedure.description: Compare the soils and relate their properties to the vegetation of each site.

observation: The river-bank soil is sandy with low moisture and water holding capacity; the garden soil is loamy; the paddy-field soil is clayey, wettest, most acidic and holds the most water.

quiz.question: When soil is shaken with water and left to settle, the layer at the bottom is:
quiz.explanation: The largest, heaviest particles settle first.

quiz.question: Which soil has the highest water holding capacity?
quiz.explanation: Fine clay particles leave tiny pores that hold water by capillarity.

quiz.question: 50.00 g of fresh soil weighs 42.00 g after drying. Its moisture content is:
Soil with pH 5.5 is:
quiz.explanation: pH below 7 is acidic.

quiz.question: Which soil is generally best for most crops?
quiz.explanation: Loam has a balance of drainage, aeration and water retention.

quiz.question: 50 g of dry soil retains 30 mL of water. Its water holding capacity is:
Why is the soil dried at 105 °C for moisture determination?

options.text: To remove all the water without burning organic matter

quiz.explanation: Just above boiling point removes the water; higher temperatures would burn organic matter.

quiz.question: Farmers add lime to acidic soils to:
quiz.explanation: Lime (calcium carbonate/oxide) neutralises soil acidity.

title: Water Analysis: pH, Clarity and Living Organisms
summary: Compare tap, pond and drain water: match pH paper, pour water over a black cross until it just disappears to measure clarity, and identify organisms in a drop under the microscope (Paramecium, Euglena, Spirogyra, Volvox, Daphnia, diatoms, bacteria).
theory:
The quality of water can be judged from simple tests.

**pH:** clean water is close to neutral (pH about 7). Decomposing organic matter in polluted water produces acids, lowering the pH.

**Clarity (transparency):** suspended particles make water **turbid**. Looking down a tube at a black cross on a white card, the depth at which the cross just disappears measures transparency: the smaller this depth, the more turbid the water. Turbidity cuts off light for aquatic plants.

**Living organisms:** a healthy pond holds many kinds of organisms: producers such as **Spirogyra**, **Volvox**, **Euglena** and **diatoms**, and consumers such as **Paramecium** and **Daphnia**. Water polluted with sewage is rich in organic matter that **bacteria** decompose, using up dissolved oxygen (a high **biochemical oxygen demand, BOD**); only a few tolerant kinds survive. Treated tap water contains no visible organisms.

procedure.title: Collect
procedure.description: Collect water from different sources (tap, pond, drain) in clean, labelled bottles.

procedure.title: pH
procedure.description: Dip universal pH paper in each sample and compare its colour with the chart.

procedure.title: Clarity
procedure.description: Stand a tall tube on a white card with a black cross. Pour in the sample slowly while looking down, and note the depth at which the cross just disappears.

procedure.title: Organisms
procedure.description: Place a drop of each sample on a slide, cover it, and identify the organisms under the microscope.

procedure.title: Compare
procedure.description: Tabulate the results and decide which sample is clean and which is polluted.

observation: Tap water is near neutral, clear and without visible organisms. Pond water is slightly turbid and has many kinds of algae and small animals. Drain water is acidic, very turbid, and has few kinds, mainly bacteria and Paramecium.

quiz.question: In the clarity test, the cross disappears at a smaller depth in water that is:
quiz.explanation: Suspended particles scatter and absorb light, so the cross is hidden sooner.

quiz.question: Which organism is a green, spindle-shaped protist with a red eyespot?
quiz.explanation: Euglena has chloroplasts, an eyespot (stigma) and a flagellum.

quiz.question: Spirogyra is recognised by its:
quiz.explanation: Its ribbon-like chloroplasts are arranged spirally.

quiz.question: Sewage-polluted water has a high BOD because:

options.text: Bacteria decomposing organic matter use up dissolved oxygen

quiz.explanation: BOD measures oxygen used by microbes to break down organic matter.

quiz.question: Daphnia, the water flea, is a:
quiz.explanation: It is a small transparent crustacean.

quiz.question: Polluted drain water usually has:

options.text: More kinds of organisms than a clean pond

quiz.explanation: Low oxygen eliminates sensitive species; tolerant bacteria and protozoa remain.

quiz.question: Diatoms have cell walls made of:
quiz.explanation: Their glassy silica walls form diatomaceous earth.

quiz.question: Which of these is a producer in a pond?
quiz.explanation: Volvox is a green alga that photosynthesises.
